author.name: Daniele Zago

entry.title: 2D Stability Selection: Design Jittering to Exclude Correlated Irrelevant Variables

link.title: 2D Stability Selection: Design Jittering to Exclude Correlated Irrelevant Variables

entry.content:
Stability Selection finds the variables that are chosen consistently across random subsamples of the data, but it can consistently choose the wrong ones. An irrelevant variable that is strongly correlated with relevant variables can be selected in many subsamples, because resampling the observations does not change the variables themselves. We call such a variable a confounder; the term refers only to this correlation and not to causal confounding. We propose 2D Stability Selection, which also adds random noise to the design matrix, at increasing noise levels, and keeps the variables that are selected throughout. On average, the added noise acts as a ridge penalty, so each fit is a noisy elastic net. This changes the conditions under which the Lasso selects the correct variables: it can restore them when a confounder would otherwise be chosen, and it can also make selection worse. For uncorrelated relevant variables we give an exact criterion for the noise levels at which the population elastic-net irrepresentable condition holds, recovery guarantees for a single fit and for the aggregated procedure, and, for thresholds above $1/2$, a bound on the expected number of false positives (under i.i.d.\ observations; its closed form also needs exchangeable irrelevant variables). In simulations, the method excludes the confounders that Stability Selection includes. In the simulated design, an elastic net used without any noise, with a fixed ridge weight or along a deterministic path, excludes the confounders as well, which suggests that for the Lasso the ridge effect, not the randomness of the noise, is responsible.

Read more

entry.title: A Bayesian approach to the survivor average causal effect in cluster-randomized crossover trials

link.title: A Bayesian approach to the survivor average causal effect in cluster-randomized crossover trials

entry.content:
In cluster-randomized crossover (CRXO) trials, groups of individuals are randomly assigned to one of two or more sequences of alternating treatments. Since clusters serve as their own control, the CRXO design is typically more statistically efficient than the usual parallel-arm design. CRXO trials are increasingly popular in many areas of health research where the number of available clusters is limited. Further, in trials among severely ill patients, researchers often want to assess the effect of treatments on secondary non-terminal outcomes, but frequently in these studies, there are patients who do not survive to have these measurements fully recorded. In this paper, we provide a causal inference framework and treatment effect estimation method for addressing truncation by death in the setting of CRXO trials. We target the survivor average causal effect (SACE) estimand, a well-defined subgroup treatment effect obtained via principal stratification. We propose causal structural assumptions and standard parametric modeling assumptions that together enable estimating the SACE within a Bayesian paradigm. We evaluate the small-sample performance of our proposed Bayesian approach for estimation of the SACE in CRXO trial settings via simulation studies. We apply our method to a previously conducted two-period cross-sectional CRXO study examining the impact of proton pump inhibitors compared to histamine-2 receptor blockers on length of hospitalization among adults requiring invasive mechanical ventilation.

Read more

entry.title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage

link.title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage

entry.content:
Online Conformal Prediction (OCP) sequentially constructs prediction sets whose average empirical coverage converges to a target level over time, for arbitrary, potentially adversarial datasets. In the multi-level setting, prediction sets are produced at $d$ coverage levels at once. Prior work argued for the use of online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which produces sets nested across levels, but with a $\sqrt{d}$ dependence in the per-level coverage convergence rate. Here, we both generalize and improve prior work. First, we show that isotonic projections can be used for the construction of multi-level online conformal prediction sets from \emph{any} online learning algorithm (not just gradient descent). Then, through a black-box reduction, we show that the linearized regret of the online algorithm itself automatically gives control over both per-level coverage and distributional consistency of multi-level predictions via Fenchel duality. Finally, by using the Weighted Interval Score, a standard scoring rule for assessing multi-level interval forecasts, we prove that these projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. We study two instantiations of our theory, $p$-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, both improving the dependence on the number of levels to $\sqrt{\log d}$ for the multi-level OCP problem. Experiments on several datasets show favorable performance compared to baselines.

Read more

entry.title: A Fully Specified Bayes Factor Range for Hypothesis Testing and Sensitivity Analysis in Process Tracing

link.title: A Fully Specified Bayes Factor Range for Hypothesis Testing and Sensitivity Analysis in Process Tracing

entry.content:
A Bayes factor can be used in process tracing to reason about the probative value of evidence for a working hypothesis against a rival (Fairfield and Charman 2022). However, relying on the researcher’s own sense of probative strength may inflate confidence in $H_1$ (Zaks 2021). We show how to fully specify a generative model of observations to compute Bayes factors in process tracing: First, researchers count the evidence. Second, they classify it as favoring either hypothesis. Third, they formalize a data-generating process that makes the evidence more expected given $H_1$ and another for a rival $H_R$. The ratio of these probabilities yields a fully specified Bayes factor. We compute two Bayes factors under different assumptions, yielding a Bayes factor range that allows researchers to decide whether the balance of evidence favors $H_1$ considering probability thresholds. Our method also facilitates sensitivity analyses of common assumptions, including those about bias and the probative weight of a smoking gun.

Read more

entry.title: A General Statistical Framework for Attention and Manipulation Checks

link.title: A General Statistical Framework for Attention and Manipulation Checks

entry.content:
Attention and manipulation checks are widely used in survey experiments to assess respondents’ attentiveness and engagement with treatment, respectively. Yet these checks are subject to measurement error, which may itself depend on treatment when checks are administered after treatment exposure. Restricting analyses to respondents who pass these checks can therefore introduce substantial bias. We propose a general statistical framework for analyzing survey experiments with pre- or post-treatment attention and manipulation checks while accounting for measurement error. We show that three separate checks suffice to identify the proportion of respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment, provided that the checks are conditionally independent among treated respondents given their true, unobserved attentiveness or manipulation status and pre-treatment covariates. Under additional mild assumptions, this result also identifies the average treatment effect among respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment. Building on these identification results, we propose an estimator that allows flexible covariate modeling and establish its asymptotic normality. Applications to framing and digital media literacy experiments demonstrate how accounting for measurement error yields treatment effect estimates that are substantively different from those obtained using conventional approaches.

Read more

entry.title: A Geometric Theory for Nonequilibrium Transformer Dynamics

link.title: A Geometric Theory for Nonequilibrium Transformer Dynamics

entry.content:
We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher–Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.

Read more

entry.title: A Review of Measurement System Uncertainty Handoffs Across the Manufacturing Decision Lifecycle

link.title: A Review of Measurement System Uncertainty Handoffs Across the Manufacturing Decision Lifecycle

entry.content:
Measurement systems generate uncertain information that downstream manufacturing decisions often consume as if fixed. This structured integrative review examines how measurement error, uncertainty, GR\&R estimates, calibration evidence, and drift information are handed off into capability inference, retrospective Phase I reference estimation, prospective Phase II monitoring, operational action, and requalification. Studies are compared by the upstream uncertain object, whether it is known, calibrated, or estimated, its propagation mechanism, the downstream decision, and the validation boundary. The synthesis distinguishes recorded production data from latent-process targets: measurement-system information calibrates limits, uncertainty statements, replication, guard bands, or losses, but does not reveal the realized random error in an individual record. Within the retained literature, measurement-to-capability and measurement-to-monitoring mechanisms are more extensively represented by model-based studies, whereas prospective evidence is thinner where statistical results must support source attribution, cost-sensitive action, and requalification. A decision-handoff spine separates measurement generation, statistical inference, and operational validation so that capability, stability, attribution, and intervention effectiveness are not conflated. The review is integrative rather than exhaustive. Its contribution is an auditable measurement-science framework that preserves provenance, information status, validity conditions, and downstream use while identifying claims that are model-supported, conditionally calibrated, or not yet operationally validated.

Read more

entry.title: A Semiparametric Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model with a Nonparametric Count Distribution for Seizure Data

link.title: A Semiparametric Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model with a Nonparametric Count Distribution for Seizure Data

entry.content:
Functional count data arise when recurrent events are recorded repeatedly over time and scientific interest centers on how event rates evolve over time and across experimental conditions. Standard mixed effects models for counts have interpretable mean structures but require a parametric conditional distribution, which can be restrictive in the presence of overdispersion, unusual zero frequencies and heavy tails. To address these challenges, we develop the functional count DPGLM (fcDPGLM), a semiparametric Bayesian mixed model that combines GLM-style regression with a nonparametric count distribution. Parametric condition-specific mean trajectories and subject-specific random effects determine the conditional mean exactly, allowing the interpretation of contrasts as usual, while remaining details of the count distribution are learned nonparametrically from the data. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models are recovered as limiting cases. A gamma completely random measure representation allows for efficient posterior simulation. In simulations mimicking a rat seizure study, fcDPGLM estimated mean contrasts as accurately as a correctly specified negative-binomial mixed model, and more accurately otherwise, and recovered zero and exceedance probabilities that the parametric models misrepresent. In the seizure study, seizure rates rise and then decline in the early period after induced status epilepticus but remain high and nearly flat in the chronic period, and rats differ substantially. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models estimate similar mean trajectories and period contrasts, but only fcDPGLM matches the observed zero frequency, variance and high-burden days.

Read more

entry.title: A Sphericity Filter for Space-Filling Designs in Noisy Experiments, with Application to Constrained Mixtures

link.title: A Sphericity Filter for Space-Filling Designs in Noisy Experiments, with Application to Constrained Mixtures

entry.content:
Space-filling designs support flexible modeling in noisy multi-response experiments, where some responses may follow simple relationships with factors even when others are complex. An individual design can nevertheless give poor joint precision for low-order effects. We use a low-order working model to guard against such designs while retaining flexibility in the final response analysis. The filter selects one complete candidate from a pool by minimizing geometric loss divided by sphericity, without altering its points. Sphericity measures the balance of the confidence ellipsoid’s principal-axis variances independently of its volume. It is the A-criterion’s shape factor in the stated coefficient coordinates (raw filtering) and the I-criterion’s shape factor in coordinates orthonormal over the prediction region (target filtering). In cube studies with quadratic least-squares and Gaussian-process fits, target filtering reduced aggregate root-mean-square prediction error by 1.4 to 3.3% relative to the geometrically best candidate in the same pool, at a median geometric-loss increase of 0.61%. Its primary benefit is tail protection: in one near-saturated setting, the worst-decile mean working-model prediction standard error fell by about a quarter, at a median geometric-loss increase of 3.2%. In constrained mixtures, raw filtering and A-optimality in physical-proportion Scheffe coordinates can emphasize extrapolated pure-component responses and blending contrasts over regional prediction. Across seven settings, A-optimal designs had 1.3–3.4 times the mean regional working-model prediction variance of I-optimal designs; target filtering improved regional working-model precision in most settings.

Read more

entry.title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence

link.title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence

entry.content:
AdamW is ubiquitous in deep learning, yet its behavior remains poorly understood. We analyze its dynamics through the lens of dynamical systems and show that AdamW admits an implicit fixed-point objective: its fixed points coincide with the stationary points of a constrained and regularized optimization problem. However, not all of these fixed points are stable under AdamW’s dynamics, and stability depends sensitively on curvature, weight decay, and momentum parameters. Even in one-dimensional settings, equilibria may be unstable, and trajectories can exhibit persistent oscillations rather than convergence to them. We further extend the analysis to higher dimensions, deriving sufficient conditions for local stability of the continuous-time dynamics, and propose a convergent modification that preserves AdamW’s fixed points. These results clarify what optimization problem AdamW is associated with, when its convergence can be expected, and how its dynamics could inspire more reliable optimizers.

Read more

entry.title: A Statistical Framework for Algorithmic Collective Action with Multiple Collectives

link.title: A Statistical Framework for Algorithmic Collective Action with Multiple Collectives

entry.content:
As learning systems increasingly shape everyday decisions, Algorithmic Collective Action (ACA), i.e., users coordinating changes to shared data to steer model behavior, offers a complement to regulator-side policy and corporate model design. Real-world collective actions have traditionally been decentralized and fragmented into multiple collectives, despite sharing overarching objectives, with each collective differing in size, strategy, and actionable goals. However, most of the ACA literature focuses on single collective settings. To address this, we propose the first comprehensive statistical framework for ACA with multiple collectives acting on the same system. In particular, we focus on collective action in classification, studying how multiple collectives can influence a classifier’s behavior. We provide quantitative statistical bounds on the success of the collectives, considering the role and the interplay of the collectives’ sizes and the alignment of their goals. We make such bounds computable by each collective with only partial knowledge of other collectives’ sizes and strategies. Finally, we numerically illustrate our framework on simulations inspired by interventions for climate adaptation in smart cities, demonstrating the usefulness of our bounds.

Read more

entry.title: ATHOS: Agreement-based Testing of Hypotheses in Overlapping Subgroups

link.title: ATHOS: Agreement-based Testing of Hypotheses in Overlapping Subgroups

entry.content:
We study confirmation of treatment benefit in a prespecified family of overlapping subgroups of a randomized trial. Maximum-statistic procedures exploit the correlation between subgroups’ statistics, but calibration decides what they protect. Re-randomization controls error exactly when treatment has no effect, but not when only an average effect is zero, whereas a multiplier bootstrap protects average effects only asymptotically. Our first result characterizes when re-randomization alone protects average effects. It reverses the arms’ weights in the statistics’ covariance, so with unequal allocation and heterogeneous effects it can overstate their correlations; in one such family of 50 subgroups, its limiting familywise error is 0.064 at nominal 0.025. We propose a step-down procedure called ATHOS, short for agreement-based testing of hypotheses in overlapping subgroups, which confirms a subgroup only when both calibrations reject it. Given assignments exchangeable within strata, ATHOS controls familywise error exactly when treatment has no effect and, under complete randomization, asymptotically for average effects, even in large families. Our second result shows that requiring agreement costs no first-order local power in balanced trials. In a null simulation with 200 patients and 1,497 subgroups, the bootstrap step-down alone made false claims in 40% of trials and ATHOS in 2.6%. In two comparisons in an HIV trial, ATHOS confirmed 188 and 73 subgroups and Holm’s procedure 179 and 62.

Read more

entry.title: A Trust Region Approach for Learning Schrödinger Bridges

link.title: A Trust Region Approach for Learning Schrödinger Bridges

entry.content:
We study the numerical approximation of Schr"{o}dinger Bridges in the setting where samples from the target distribution are unavailable and only an unnormalized target density is given. In this regime, the widely used iterative proportional fitting (IPF) procedure (and its variants) often exhibits severe numerical instabilities, stemming from ill-conditioned underlying control problems and from the fact that the optimal solution may lie far from the initialization. To address these issues, we propose a trust region variant of IPF that constrains successive updates to remain at a fixed Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current iterate. This restriction significantly improves numerical stability. Moreover, we show that the resulting method admits an interpretation as a mirror descent scheme with an adaptively chosen step size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging sampling tasks.

Read more

entry.title: A Unified Framework for Robust Blinded Sample Size Re-estimation Based on Nuisance Parameters

link.title: A Unified Framework for Robust Blinded Sample Size Re-estimation Based on Nuisance Parameters

entry.content:
Blinded sample size re-estimation aims to mitigate uncertainty in nuisance parameters at the design stage while preserving the integrity of the trial. It allows the required sample size to be updated without revealing treatment assignments and thereby reduces the risk of an inappropriate sample size. Although numerous procedures have been proposed for different outcome types, a unified framework is still lacking. We therefore develop a general framework for blinded sample size re-estimation based on nuisance parameters. Within this general framework, we develop robust methods to reduce the influence of extreme observations. The proposed framework combines asymptotically linear estimators for the parameter of interest with robust Z-estimators for nuisance parameters, thereby unifying a broad class of existing procedures through different choices of estimating functions. We also propose a general principle for constructing nuisance parameters that can be estimated from blinded data. The proposed framework is supported by asymptotic theory showing that the type I error rate converges to the nominal level under regularity conditions. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method maintains reliable type I error control across a range of settings, including contaminated data and small pilot sample sizes. Compared with existing blinded and unblinded methods, the proposed framework is more flexible and less sensitive to outliers. A clinical trial application illustrates its practical utility.

entry.title: Adaptive Budgeted Data Acquisition for Robust Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Loggers

link.title: Adaptive Budgeted Data Acquisition for Robust Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Loggers

entry.content:
We consider off-policy evaluation when additional data can be purchased from several existing logging policies (or loggers) with heterogeneous costs per observation. While existing work on multiple loggers presumes a fixed number of observations from each logger, we study how to allocate a limited budget across them sequentially to evaluate a finite class of target policies. We propose Adaptive Greedy, an algorithm that purchases observations sequentially from the affordable logger that has the most cost-normalized variance reduction across the target policies. It turns out that each such purchase is an ‘approximate conditional-gradient step’ for the corresponding design problem. Under mild assumptions, we establish that the empirical allocation converges almost surely to the optimal design at an explicit rate. We also derive the asymptotic normality of the final pooled estimator and show that it attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Simulations and a semi-synthetic application based on the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 show that Adaptive Greedy outperforms standard allocation strategies, remains accurate if stopped early, and matches the final accuracy of repeated integer programming at a fraction of its computational cost.

Read more

entry.title: Adaptive Inference for Functionals of M-Estimands

link.title: Adaptive Inference for Functionals of M-Estimands

entry.content:
Reinforcement learning and contextual bandit algorithms have become increasingly common in sequential decision-making applications. When these methods are deployed in high-stakes domains, there is growing interest not only in learning effective policies, but also in conducting statistical inference for quantities learned under adaptive data collection. However, classical procedures applied naively in these settings can fail: even when estimators are unbiased, their variance becomes path-dependent and as a result may not be asymptotically normal. A growing literature has emerged to ameliorate this problem, but solutions tend to be problem specific and often rely on correct specification of a working model. In this work, we develop a unified framework for constructing asymptotically valid confidence intervals to cover smooth functionals of nonparametric M-estimands under adaptive sampling. Under Neyman orthogonality, we provide two novel methods for performing inference: (1) a self-normalized statistic based on the realized quadratic variation of the influence function and (2) a statistic using a plug-in estimate of the conditional variance based on reweighted influence function increments. Our results allow for flexible nonparametric estimation of nuisance parameters and remain valid under model misspecification. Our theory is supported by a simulation study for a dynamic pricing application which demonstrates that this method can produce asymptotically valid confidence intervals where standard methods fail.

entry.title: Algorithm-aware Statistical Inference in High-dimensional Estimating Equations

link.title: Algorithm-aware Statistical Inference in High-dimensional Estimating Equations

entry.content:
Iterative algorithms are integral to many statistical procedures, whereas sampling uncertainty along their iteration is generally not quantified. We develop simultaneous inference for discrete trajectories generated from high-dimensional estimating equations, with iteration-specific population estimands that preserve algorithmic regularization. Our proposed fixed-Jacobian bootstrap propagates perturbations along the observed trajectory without repeatedly running the original nonlinear algorithm. We establish uniform first-order expansions and bootstrap validity over possibly infinite sets of contrasts and iterations under stability, entropy and moment conditions. Simulations in sparse linear regression, paired Fisher discrimination, and temporal-difference learning demonstrate accurate simultaneous coverage. A micro-randomized trial application illustrates inference for a treatment trajectory with participant-level clustering.

Read more

entry.title: A lift for input-convex neural net training

link.title: A lift for input-convex neural net training

entry.content:
Input-convex neural nets parametrize the convex potentials of density models and transport maps, and their convexity requires the inter-layer weights to be non-negative. Projected gradient descent enforces this by projecting after each step, and due to mini-batch noise the boundary is re-crossed indefinitely, which leads to an active set the projection never identifies. The differentiable alternative, direct softplus, optimizes a free latent weight through a softplus positivity map. Where that latent weight is well below zero, the derivative of the map is exponentially small and scales down both the gradient and its noise. We call this region the shoulder, and a weight that reaches it therefore barely moves and stays for an exponentially long time. We propose the lift, which replaces the free latent weight by a learnable slack plus the output of a hypernetwork that reads a permutation-invariant summary of the training batch. The latent weight then varies with the same batch that forms the gradient, so the two are coupled. We show that this coupling adds a term to the variance of the update at first order, and that the slack, the batch dependence, and the shared batch are each needed for it. Where the coupling aligns positively with the loss curvature, a weight on the shoulder crosses the barriers of the loss sooner under the lift than under direct softplus, also under preconditioned stochastic gradient descent. We compare the lift with the two existing methods on several applications. Where a constrained weight of direct softplus reaches the shoulder, the lift fits the target more closely than direct softplus and reaches the same reconstruction about three times sooner. Where almost none reaches it, the methods agree.

Read more

entry.title: Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for Nonlinear Matrix Decompositions

link.title: Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for Nonlinear Matrix Decompositions

entry.content:
We present an algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for solving nonlinear matrix decompositions (NMD). Given an input matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and a factorization rank $r \ll \min(m, n)$, NMD seeks matrices $W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$ and $H \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n}$ such that $X \approx f(WH)$, where $f$ is an element-wise nonlinear function. We evaluate our method on several representative nonlinear models: the rectified linear unit activation $f(x) = \max(0, x)$, suitable for nonnegative sparse data approximation, the component-wise square $f(x) = x^2$, applicable to probabilistic circuit representation, and the MinMax transform $f(x) = \min(b, \max(a, x))$, relevant for recommender systems. The proposed framework flexibly supports diverse loss functions, including least squares, $\ell_1$ norm, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and can be readily extended to other nonlinearities and metrics. We illustrate the applicability, efficiency, and adaptability of the approach on real-world datasets, highlighting its potential for a broad range of applications.

entry.title: A method to automatically discover symbolic local learning rules

link.title: A method to automatically discover symbolic local learning rules

entry.content:
We present a general method for discovering symbolic local learning rules that can replace backpropagation, applicable, in principle, to any deep learning architecture and task. The method automatically discovers local loss functions specific to each layer by (1) constructing a dictionary of monomials of local tensor variables, inspired by Penrose diagram notation, (2) regressing over coefficients weighting these monomials to build layerwise polynomial losses whose gradients together minimize a target global loss. We test the method on classification, reconstruction, and self-supervised learning tasks with small multilayer networks and minimal datasets. Across all tasks, the discovered rules induce non-trivial interactions between layers, which lead to significant reductions in the corresponding global losses. Furthermore, the method selects sparse combinations of monomials, finding local rules that are more interpretable than those generated by MLP-based alternatives. The potential implications of our method range from energy-efficient deep learning to the discovery of biologically plausible learning mechanisms.

Read more

entry.title: Amortized Bayesian Experimental Design with In-Context Knowledge Conditioning

link.title: Amortized Bayesian Experimental Design with In-Context Knowledge Conditioning

entry.content:
Amortized Bayesian experimental design (BED) enables real-time design strategies by shifting acquisition cost offline, but existing methods remain tied to the prior and task distribution they were trained on and cannot exploit additional information available at deployment. We introduce in-context amortized BED with unified knowledge encoding (IMBUE), a BED framework that admits external knowledge at deployment through a unified in-context interface. IMBUE accepts two forms of such knowledge without retraining, namely user-specified prior knowledge and observations from previous instances of the experiment. Both are encoded as additional input tokens and processed in-context with the accumulated observations by a shared Transformer, and a learned reliability filter scores each external token against the observations and excludes inconsistent ones. Across four benchmarks, IMBUE accelerates early-stage information acquisition when the external knowledge is reliable, and remains close to the no-external baseline when it is not.

Read more

entry.title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting

link.title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting

entry.content:
Hierarchical Bayesian models pool measurements, but with the forward model in the likelihood every posterior evaluation costs one forward solve per cell. To reduce this cost, we introduce a simulation-based inference framework in which a triangular transport-map likelihood, trained once per design, serves every cell. We apply it to infer wetting properties from photographs of a stable hole in a thin liquid film. The hole’s radius depends, through the nonlinear Young-Laplace equation, on the contact angle and capillary length. One photograph gives rank-one information about them, so we pool many in a hierarchical model whose cells, each a substrate at one volume setting, share the apparatus geometry and the noise scale. A design fixes the number of substrates, the volume settings and the photographs per cell. The map’s posteriors agree with direct sampling of the forward model in the wetting properties at a synthetic validation design, and less closely at a larger synthetic scaling design. At the validation design, simulation-based calibration detects no departure for any parameter. There, the map needs several hundred times fewer forward-model evaluations than direct sampling with a gradient-free ensemble sampler for a single posterior, and about five orders of magnitude fewer over a calibration study of 200 posteriors. On real photographs its posterior agrees with direct sampling and is consistent with the measured radii. Trained offline, the amortized map turns new photographs into a posterior with no forward solve. It is thus a major step toward measuring wetting properties in situ without disturbing the liquid.

Read more

entry.title: Amortized Vine Copulas for High-Dimensional Density and Information Estimation

link.title: Amortized Vine Copulas for High-Dimensional Density and Information Estimation

entry.content:
Modeling high-dimensional dependencies while keeping likelihoods tractable re- mains challenging. Classical vine copulas provide an explicit dependence structure but require repeated, costly bivariate fitting. We propose Vine Denoising Copula (VDC)1, an amortized estimator for simplified vines on continuous data. VDC trains a single bivariate denoising network on simulated copulas and reuses it across all vine edges. For each edge, the network maps an empirical histogram to a density grid, and iterative proportional fitting approximately enforces uniform grid marginals. The predicted densities and cached conditional transforms support stan- dard vine recursion, likelihood evaluation, sampling, and information estimation. This retains the classical vine factorization while replacing repeated per-edge fitting with reusable neural inference. Across synthetic and real-data benchmarks, VDC combines accurate bivariate density estimation, competitive information estimates, and faster high-dimensional vine fitting after pretraining. Performance varies across datasets; finite grid resolution and conditional prediction remain limitations. The explicit fitted structure supports edge- and tree-level information decomposition, making repeated dependence analysis more practical.

Read more

entry.title: An Exact Marginal Likelihood for Inference under Careless Responding

link.title: An Exact Marginal Likelihood for Inference under Careless Responding

entry.content:
Careless or insufficient-effort responding threatens the validity of self-report measurement. Mixture models for careless responding specify its form, and screening rules and robust methods depend on a threshold or tuning constant with no direct meaning in terms of careless responses. We propose ExHuber, a Bayesian method for inference on the engaged population under Huber’s contamination model, in which an unknown proportion of responses comes from a contaminating distribution of unspecified form instead of the structural model. With a finite support of responses, such as the values of a scale score, a Dirichlet prior and a Beta prior on the contaminating distribution and its proportion yield a closed-form exact marginal likelihood of the structural parameters. Under a prior favoring a contaminating distribution on a few values, we show that the posterior of the structural parameters is consistent when careless responses occupy few values of the support, without knowing which values. Dynamic programming evaluates the marginal likelihood and its gradient at a cost quadratic in the sample size, which enables gradient-based sampling. Simulations from graded response models show accurate inference under straightlining and repeated response patterns, and an application to Big Five scales estimates the engaged mean of each scale.

Read more

entry.title: An Exact Poisson Mixture Representation of Siler Remaining Life Expectancy

link.title: An Exact Poisson Mixture Representation of Siler Remaining Life Expectancy

entry.content:
The Siler model describes mortality from birth to old age as the sum of a declining immaturity hazard, a constant background hazard, and an increasing senescence hazard. Its remaining life expectancy has no known closed form, and numerical evaluation alone does not reveal how the immaturity hazard enters it. We show that the remaining-lifetime distribution at age $x$ is Gompertz–Makeham with a Poisson-distributed Makeham term. Successive Makeham terms differ by the rate at which immaturity mortality declines, and the Poisson mean is the cumulative immaturity hazard remaining after age $x$. In a latent-clock construction, individuals carry a Poisson number of constant-rate clocks, and selection removes those carrying more clocks first. Integrating the mixture yields an exact series for remaining life expectancy with a closed-form truncation bound. The life expectancy lost to immaturity mortality is close to the probability of carrying a clock times life expectancy with that hazard removed, with a closed-form error bound. In annual fits to Swedish female mortality, this loss at birth fell from 4.3 years in 1900 to less than 0.01 years in 2020, a decline equal to 15\% of the gain in life expectancy at birth, and the approximation was always within 0.06 years.

Read more

entry.title: An Exploratory Pilot Analysis of Paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 SPR Sensorgrams: Retained Response, Early Shape, and Complementarity

link.title: An Exploratory Pilot Analysis of Paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 SPR Sensorgrams: Retained Response, Early Shape, and Complementarity

entry.content:
We conduct a retrospective exploratory pilot analysis of paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 surface plasmon resonance (SPR) trajectories, examining retained response, dual-marker fusion, and additional early-shape information. Numerical matching links the original exports to previously quality-selected data: 69 files represent 68 distinct source column pairs from 10 cancer and 10 healthy study patients. Existing exclusions and truncations are preserved. All 20 patients contribute to development and exploration; no independent validation cohort is available. Because historical per-scan manual alignment offsets are unavailable, the numerical comparisons are conditional on separately documented candidate response-transition intervals rather than verified injection-event times. Patient-level paired comparisons, leave-pair-out internal assessment, empirical false-positive budgets, and timing sensitivity are implemented in reproducible Python code. Under candidate alignment, the dual-marker retained-response sum has an apparent AUC of 0.570, with a fixed-score bootstrap 95% interval of [0.300, 0.820]. In the nested 13-patient shape subset, retention alone and the fixed 85:15 retention-shape score both have AUC 0.619; the small paired increment changes direction across the -1,0,+1 minute shift scenarios. At a same-sample budget of two false positives among ten controls, dual-marker retention identifies four cancer cases, compared with two for PD-L1 and three for Siglec-15. Analytical bounds describe feature stability under stated measurement assumptions but do not identify the cause of weak discrimination. The study provides a traceable analysis framework and operating-point hypotheses for independent evaluation; the small development cohort does not establish diagnostic utility or a reliable fusion or shape advantage.

entry.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing

link.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing

entry.content:
Statistical data editing in official statistics must restore consistency while limiting changes to observed data. Exact minimum-change correction can be computationally demanding. This paper develops a general framework for structured data whose dependencies admit a normalized acyclic routing representation. It connects routing metadata and explicitly specified semantic edits to logical admissibility, violation diagnosis, and correction. Under stated record semantics, the generated Horn theory characterizes admissibility without materializing its deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the origin of each requirement and identify the variables that can affect a violation. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible records within the specified domain. This characterization is independent of the correction procedure and provides both an objective for correction and a certificate: a verified zero-energy output is admissible and globally minimizes violation energy within its permitted candidate domain. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates based on attained lower bounds. A household survey application illustrates the construction, the verification of admissible corrections, and minimum-cost certification for a subset of outputs. The framework supports traceable validation and correction in official statistics, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.

Read more

With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible records within the specified domain. This characterization is independent of the correction procedure and provides both an objective for correction and a certificate: a verified zero-energy output is admissible and globally minimizes violation energy within its permitted candidate domain. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates based on attained lower bounds. A household survey application illustrates the construction, the verification of admissible corrections, and minimum-cost certification for a subset of outputs. The framework supports traceable validation and correction in official statistics, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.

entry.title: Analysis increments for model bias diagnosis and correction: Theoretical foundations

link.title: Analysis increments for model bias diagnosis and correction: Theoretical foundations

entry.content:
A common method for diagnosing and correcting model bias in weather and climate prediction is based on analysis increments: the difference between the analysis and the forecast at each data assimilation cycle. Their time average is used to estimate and correct the bias, and machine learning is increasingly used to map the forecast state to the increments, giving a state-dependent correction. Despite its widespread use, the method lacks theoretical foundations. We first analyse a Kalman filter whose forecast model has a constant bias. We show what the averaged increment measures, and prove that iterating the correction removes all of the bias seen through the observations; for linear dynamics, no method can identify the rest. We then extend the analysis to state-dependent biases. For linear dynamics, each increment records the model error over the filter’s memory, as seen through the observations. We use this to determine what the increments measure when averaged over a long period, averaged over periods with similar slowly varying conditions, and used without averaging, as in machine-learned corrections. Numerical experiments confirm the theory for a linear model and suggest that its main conclusions carry over to the nonlinear Lorenz ‘96 model, including for a correction learned by a neural network.

Read more

entry.title: Anchored Extra-Proximal Methods: Optimal Higher-Order Methods for Monotone Inclusion Problems

link.title: Anchored Extra-Proximal Methods: Optimal Higher-Order Methods for Monotone Inclusion Problems

entry.content:
We characterize, up to logarithmic factors, the optimal higher-order oracle complexity of finding approximate solutions to composite monotone inclusion problems, formed by the sum of a smooth single-valued monotone operator and a maximal monotone set-valued operator. We introduce the Anchored Extra-Proximal (AEP) framework, which combines an anchored extrapolation step with an inexact anchored proximal update satisfying a relative-error condition. This framework recovers the composite Fast Extragradient method in the first-order setting and yields natural higher-order extensions through Taylor approximations of the smooth operator at the extrapolated point. For every $p\geq 2$, assuming that the $(p-1)$th derivative of the single-valued operator is $L_p$-Lipschitz continuous and the initial distance to a solution is at most $R$, we combine AEP with a bisection line search to obtain a $p$th-order method that attains a tangent residual of at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}((L_p R^{p}/\varepsilon)^{\frac{2}{3p-1}})$ oracle calls. We complement this result with a worst-case lower bound of $\Omega((L_p R^p/\varepsilon)^{\frac{2}{3p-1}})$ for every deterministic algorithm in the $p$th-order oracle model, without imposing any prescribed update structure. For the subclass of smooth nonexpansive fixed-point problems, we further establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\min{R/\varepsilon, {(L_p R^{p}/\varepsilon)}^{\frac{2}{3p-1}}})$. By choosing between AEP and Halpern iteration, we match this lower bound up to logarithmic factors, thereby also settling the deterministic oracle complexity of smooth nonexpansive fixed-point problems.

entry.title: An iterated-logarithm price of anytime validity for log-optimal e-processes

link.title: An iterated-logarithm price of anytime validity for log-optimal e-processes

entry.content:
Log-optimal e-variables at fixed horizons, also called num'eraires, have been conjectured to almost'' form an e-process for exponential-family null hypotheses. A related open question is whether an e-process can attain the optimal e-power at every horizon up to a bounded loss. Given a final horizon, we study the minimax regret of e-processes relative to the num\'eraires at all times up to it. For the Gaussian location null and the composite alternative of Gaussian distributions with a smaller variance and an unknown location, we show that the minimax regret in the worst case over the location grows like the iterated logarithm of the final horizon. A single e-process attains this rate at every horizon. This growth answers the question negatively. It also refutes the conjecture ifalmost’’ means a regret bounded uniformly over horizons. For this Gaussian location problem, we thus exhibit the frontier precisely: the minimax regret is bounded if and only if the alternatives have at least the variance of the null.

Read more

entry.title: Annealing in variational inference mitigates mode collapse: A theoretical study on Gaussian mixtures

link.title: Annealing in variational inference mitigates mode collapse: A theoretical study on Gaussian mixtures

entry.content:
Mode collapse, the failure to capture one or more modes when targeting a multimodal distribution, is a central challenge in modern variational inference. In this work, we provide a mathematical analysis of annealing based strategies for mitigating mode collapse in a tractable setting: learning a Gaussian mixture, where mode collapse is known to arise. Leveraging a low dimensional summary statistics description, we precisely characterize the interplay between the initial temperature and the annealing rate, and derive a sharp formula for the probability of mode collapse. Our analysis shows that an appropriately chosen annealing scheme can robustly prevent mode collapse. Finally, we present numerical evidence that these theoretical tradeoffs qualitatively extend to neural network based models, RealNVP normalizing flows, providing guidance for designing annealing strategies mitigating mode collapse in practical variational inference pipelines.

Read more

entry.title: A non-parametric estimator for excess recurrent events

link.title: A non-parametric estimator for excess recurrent events

entry.content:
Measuring disease burden is an important part of both public health research and health economics. Some measures of disease burden, such as hospitalisations, are made up of recurrent events. Assessing what events are related to a particular disease is however non-trivial. We extend the notion of relative survival to recurrent events by developing a novel non-parametric estimator. The estimator combines data from some cohort with aggregated population level data to estimate the number of excess recurrent events. Using empirical process theory, we show that the estimator converges weakly to a mean zero Gaussian process under mild regularity conditions, and provide a consistent estimator for the covariance function. We also evaluate the finite sample properties of the estimator through simulations and provide a practical example using data from Swedish patients with rectal cancer.

Read more

entry.title: Asymptotically Log-Optimal Bayes-Assisted Confidence Sequences for Bounded Means

link.title: Asymptotically Log-Optimal Bayes-Assisted Confidence Sequences for Bounded Means

entry.content:
Confidence sequences based on test martingales provide time-uniform uncertainty quantification for the mean of bounded i.i.d. observations without parametric distributional assumptions. Their practical efficiency, however, depends strongly on the choice of martingale updates, and many existing constructions do not exploit prior information about plausible data-generating distributions or mean values. We propose a Bayes-assisted framework that uses a Bayesian working predictive model to adaptively construct confidence sequences. For each candidate mean and time point, the predictive distribution selects, among valid one-step martingale factors, the update maximising predictive expected log-growth; validity is therefore preserved even when the prior or working model is misspecified. We prove that if the predictive distribution is Wasserstein-consistent, the resulting procedure is asymptotically log-optimal, matching the per-sample log-growth of an oracle procedure with access to the true distribution. We instantiate the framework using robust predictives based on Dirichlet-process mixtures and Bayesian exponentially tilted empirical likelihood. Experiments on synthetic data, sequential best-arm identification for LLM evaluation, and prediction-powered inference show that informative priors can substantially reduce confidence-sequence width and sampling effort while retaining anytime-valid coverage.

Read more

entry.title: Attention as In-Context Empirical Bayes: A Two-Stage View via Particle Dynamics

link.title: Attention as In-Context Empirical Bayes: A Two-Stage View via Particle Dynamics

entry.content:
We study minimal attention-only transformers under all-token corruption and show they admit a two-stage empirical Bayes interpretation. A single attention step computes a kernel-weighted posterior mean with respect to the empirical distribution defined by the context. Depth refines this distribution through particle dynamics (Stage 1), while a long-range skip-connection carries the noisy input as a query for posterior inference (Stage 2), revealing distinct statistical roles for depth and attention residuals. The framework isolates a minimal setting in which the context itself induces a depth-dependent energy landscape governing in-context inference. We show that effective denoising can emerge without an explicit noise schedule: a fixed kernel bandwidth and finite integration horizon suffice, yielding a principled depth-noise relationship. We further establish a posterior-mean recovery guarantee for Gaussian priors, showing the empirical estimator converges to the Bayes-optimal predictor under sequential asymptotic conditions. Connecting these dynamics to reverse-diffusion limits, our results provide a statistical interpretation of attention as in-context inference via sample-based posterior estimation, without explicit density modeling.

Read more

entry.title: Attention in Constant Time: Vashista Sparse Attention for Long-Context Decoding with Exponential Guarantees

link.title: Attention in Constant Time: Vashista Sparse Attention for Long-Context Decoding with Exponential Guarantees

entry.content:
Large language models spend most of their inference cost on attention over long contexts, yet empirical behavior suggests that only a small subset of tokens meaningfully contributes to each query. We formalize this phenomenon by modeling attention as a projection onto the convex hull of key vectors and analyzing its entropic (softmax-like) relaxation. Our main theoretical contribution is a face-stability theorem showing that, under a strict complementarity margin (a support gap (\Delta) certified by KKT multipliers), entropic attention concentrates on a constant-size active face: the total mass assigned to inactive tokens decays exponentially as (\exp(-\Omega(\Delta/\varepsilon))), while the error on the active face scales linearly in the temperature/regularization parameter (\varepsilon). This yields a practical criterion for when sparse long-context decoding is safe and provides a principled knob to trade accuracy for compute. Building on these guarantees, we introduce Vashista Sparse Attention, a drop-in mechanism that maintains a small candidate set per query through a paging-style context selection strategy compatible with modern inference stacks. Across long-context evaluations, we observe stable constant-size effective support, strong wall-clock speedups, and minimal quality degradation in the regimes predicted by the support-gap diagnostics. Finally, we discuss deployment implications for privacy-sensitive and air-gapped settings, where interchangeable attention modules enable predictable latency and cost without external retrieval dependencies.

Read more

entry.title: Automating structural reliability analysis with a multi-agent large language model framework

link.title: Automating structural reliability analysis with a multi-agent large language model framework

entry.content:
Structural reliability analysis supports the design and safety assessment of buildings and civil infrastructure but requires specialized expertise throughout the workflow. This study presents a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework that automates component-level reliability analysis from a natural-language problem statement to interpreted estimates of the reliability index and failure probability. Specialized agents handle problem formulation, method planning, code generation, execution, and result interpretation, with human confirmation at key decision points. Numerical reliability estimates are not generated by an LLM; instead, they are obtained solely through deterministic execution of validated solvers. This design mitigates the risk of hallucinated numerical outputs and supports reproducibility. The Method Planner is fine-tuned using quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) for a priori reliability-method category selection. The framework uses open-weight models and supports local execution without closed APIs. Results show that it lowers the expertise barrier to structural reliability assessment while preserving computational trustworthiness.

Read more

entry.title: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks

link.title: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks

entry.content:
Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. Given an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping, we show that potential outcomes admit a nonparametric decomposition into direct, spillover, and treatment–spillover interaction components. This decomposition provides a common coordinate system for nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric models of finite-population potential outcomes. For a given potential-outcome model, we define two classes of estimands. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as direct and total treatment effects, contrast potential outcomes under fixed treatment–exposure conditions. Expected causal effects (ECEs), such as expected direct and indirect effects, contrast expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy. For both classes, we bound the variance of the canonical Horvitz–Thompson estimator by three terms: a diagonal weight term, a term from overlapping interference neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term. Our upper and lower bounds show that under graph-unaware designs, nonparametric design-unbiased estimation of ACEs can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the interference degree, whereas polynomial growth can suffice for design-aligned ECEs. Under neighborhood interference, we construct graph-aware independent-set designs with variance bounds polynomial in the maximum degree for direct and total treatment effects on every graph, whereas graph cluster randomization can incur worst-case variance exponential in the degree.

entry.title: A weighted edge-count two-sample test for multivariate and object data

link.title: A weighted edge-count two-sample test for multivariate and object data

entry.content:
Two-sample tests for multivariate data and non-Euclidean data are widely used in many fields. Parametric tests are mostly restrained to certain types of data that meets the assumptions of the parametric models. In this paper, we study a nonparametric testing procedure that utilizes graphs representing the similarity among observations. It can be applied to any data types as long as an informative similarity measure on the sample space can be defined. The classic test based on a similarity graph has a problem when the two sample sizes are different. We solve the problem by applying appropriate weights to different components of the classic test statistic. The new test exhibits substantial power gains in simulation studies. Its asymptotic permutation null distribution is derived and shown to work well under finite samples, facilitating its application to large datasets. The new test is illustrated through an analysis on a real dataset of network data.

Read more

entry.title: BSTabDiff: Block-Subunit Diffusion Priors for High-Dimensional Tabular Data Generation

link.title: BSTabDiff: Block-Subunit Diffusion Priors for High-Dimensional Tabular Data Generation

entry.content:
High-Dimensional Low-Sample Size (HDLSS) tabular domains (e.g., omics) are characterized by $n \ll m$, where $n$ = number of samples, and $m$ = number of features. Such domains often exhibit strong local correlation groups, sparse cross-group dependencies, heavy-tailed non-Gaussian marginals, heteroscedastic noise, and structured missingness, making direct density learning in $\mathbb{R}^m$ ill-conditioned since $n \ll m$. We propose BSTabDiff, a block-subunit generative framework that partitions the $m$ observed features into $M$ latent blocks ($M \ll m$) and generates each block via a shared low-dimensional subunit variable, concentrating global dependence learning in the compact block-latent space $\mathbb{R}^M$ while decoding to the full feature space with copula-driven dependence, flexible per-feature marginals, and explicit missingness mechanisms. BSTabDiff can induce a data-driven feature ordering and block construction before latent partitioning, allowing the model to better align with local dependency structure when such organization is beneficial. BSTabDiff supports modern deep priors on block latents, including diffusion and normalizing flows, enabling stable synthesis and controllable benchmark generation in the HDLSS regime. Empirically, BSTabDiff produces more realistic and more stable high-dimensional synthetic data when compared with unstructured tabular generators on HDLSS data.

Read more

entry.title: Balanced State Subspaces with Spectral Rank Allocation for Mamba-2 State Compression

link.title: Balanced State Subspaces with Spectral Rank Allocation for Mamba-2 State Compression

entry.content:
Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune coordinates with per-channel scores. Trained states are nearly rank-one and bias-like, aligned with the mean write; but the output’s energy spans an order of magnitude more directions. Per-channel scores see only the diagonal of the write–read operator, so they cannot select the subspace that governs the input–output map, which is a rotation of the coordinates. We therefore propose \method{}, which keeps that subspace by applying balanced truncation exactly via Mamba-2’s scalar-identity transition. Layers differ just as sharply: most are bias-dominated, while the few that carry long-range associations are the flattest and need most of their state. We therefore introduce \spar{}, which redistributes a fixed total rank budget across layers according to the Hankel spectrum. On Mamba-2 checkpoints from 130M to 2.7B, \method{}+\spar{} halves the state at an average cost of $0.3$ WikiText-2 perplexity points, against $1.6$ for GHOST, while retaining $97\%$ of the dense model’s five-digit in-context recall. At a quarter of the state, giving every layer the same rank keeps $5\%$ of that recall and \spar{} $77\%$, for a $7\%$ perplexity cost.

Read more

entry.title: BayesJudge: Uncertainty-Aware Bayesian Meta-Evaluation of Human and LLM Judgments

link.title: BayesJudge: Uncertainty-Aware Bayesian Meta-Evaluation of Human and LLM Judgments

entry.content:
AI evaluation pipelines often produce conflicting judgments rather than clean labels. Yet existing methods largely collapse disagreement into a single hard label. As a result, item ambiguity, rater biases, and the position preferences of LLM judges are erased together: evaluation outcomes appear deterministic while concealing the underlying uncertainty, and may even systematically favor one response. This conflict is especially acute in pairwise LLM evaluation. We propose \textbf{BayesJudge}, an online Bayesian meta-evaluation layer for conflicting human-LLM judgment streams. BayesJudge treats the latent preference of each item as a latent variable and jointly models two sources of evaluator bias: rater-specific confusion matrices for human annotation bias, and an explicit order parameter for the position preference of LLM judges, thereby separating response quality from evaluator bias. We derive an exact online posterior recursion and adopt a scalable Rao-Blackwellized assumed-density sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) approximation for streaming inference. Consequently, each comparison yields not a single hard label but a posterior distribution over each response winning (as well as a tie or ambiguity state), together with posterior estimates of the bias parameters, making evaluation uncertainty explicit and quantifiable. On synthetic data, BayesJudge accurately recovers human annotation biases and LLM position biases online, and strictly outperforms variants that freeze either bias channel in held-out predictive log-likelihood. On the real-world SummEval dataset, BayesJudge detects systematic order effects in LLM judgments, distinguishes the behavioral signatures of experts and crowdworkers without rater metadata, and yields posterior uncertainty that reflects genuine human disagreement. Our code is available at https://github.com/Killerofthecard/BayesJudge.git

entry.title: Bayesian Optimization on Function Spaces via Sparse RKHS Manifolds

link.title: Bayesian Optimization on Function Spaces via Sparse RKHS Manifolds

entry.content:
Bayesian Optimization (BO) has become an established methodology for minimizing black-box functions of a vector input. Often, however, this parameter vector arises from the discretization of an inherently functional relationship. Several recent articles have considered the Functional Bayesian Optimization (FBO) setting, in which the variable to be optimized is not a member of a finite dimensional vector space, but rather an infinite dimensional function space. In this work, we propose $L^0$ Manifold Optimization (L0MO), a simple approach to FBO which searches the subset of a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) consisting of functions with a sparse representation in the kernel functions, optimizing both the kernel locations and their coefficients. We discuss in detail the relationship between our method and existing ones, providing a unifying lens through which to view prior works. To assess our method against the state of the art, we conduct an extensive computational study, and along the way develop a novel set of benchmark test functions which port standard finite-dimensional ones to the infinite dimensional domain. Our experiments demonstrate that, on balance, the proposed method achieves superior performance across a wide range of test benchmarks.

Read more

entry.title: Bayesian Wombling for Tracking Invasive Species

link.title: Bayesian Wombling for Tracking Invasive Species

entry.content:
This paper develops Bayesian wombling, or boundary analysis for tracking invasive species. We focus on three invasive species of concern in North America: Lycorma delicatula, Adelges tsugae, and Microstegium vimineum. We aim to demonstrate the applicability of wombling for supporting invasive pest management activities. In spatial science wombling is used widely to track regions of rapid change within the spatial reference domain. We use Gaussian process models for point-referenced spatial data followed by predictive inference on rates of change over curves using line integrals. We extend the wombling model based Bayesian inference framework to feature simple analytic forms that avoid high dimensional quadrature while offering uncertainty quantification over curvilinear spatial boundaries.

Read more

entry.title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series

link.title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series

entry.content:
Series in a macroeconomic panel are almost all correlated with one another, which makes correlation a poor guide to which pairs are directly linked. For example, Treasury rates at different maturities are all highly correlated, yet a short and a long rate may be related only through the rates at maturities between them; similarly, sectors of the economy such as output, employment, prices, and interest rates may be related directly or only through other series. Both are questions about the inverse covariance matrix. Recovering it from quarterly data is difficult: contemporaneous dependence is entangled with temporal dynamics, the innovations remain densely dependent once those dynamics are removed, and the number of series is comparable to the number of quarters observed. We propose VAPOR (Vector Autoregressive Precision factOR), a Bayesian model that estimates vector autoregressive dynamics jointly with a factor-structured innovation precision matrix, inferring the partial correlations directly from the fitted precision rather than imposing a zero pattern. Applied to 100 quarterly FRED-QD series, VAPOR learns from the data that each Treasury rate is directly related only to the rates at adjacent maturities, places all 26 selected dependencies within a single FRED-QD group, and attains the lowest held-out prediction error among the estimators compared.

Read more

entry.title: Bayesian transfer for offline Q-learning with multi-task Gaussian processes

link.title: Bayesian transfer for offline Q-learning with multi-task Gaussian processes

entry.content:
Offline reinforcement learning can benefit from data collected in related tasks, yet indiscriminate knowledge transfer may lead to negative transfer under task mismatch and limited target-data coverage. We propose a target-aware Bayesian transfer framework for offline Q-learning based on multi-task Gaussian processes that jointly model task-specific Q-functions. Source tasks are assessed using target predictive evidence and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), while posterior uncertainty and behavior-supported action sets guide conservative Bellman updates and policy extraction. To account for the dependence induced by Bellman bootstrapping, we distinguish Bellman innovations from bootstrap errors and establish stability and predictive source-selection results under explicit regularity conditions. We further derive selection-adaptive posterior contraction and offline policy-performance bounds, identifying the structural conditions under which source information can be pooled to achieve minimax-optimal rates in a shared-function Gaussian sequence experiment. Simulation studies with heterogeneous source tasks demonstrate improved target Q-function estimation and reduced material negative transfer compared with indiscriminate source pooling. An application to human decision-making data further shows higher average expected immediate payoff than both target-only learning and matched-size random source selection. These results highlight the benefits of combining target-aware source selection with uncertainty-aware conservative learning for reliable and sample-efficient offline reinforcement learning.

Read more

entry.title: Beyond Discrete Ancestry Groups: Distribution-Aware In-Context Learning for Cancer Outcome Prediction Across the Genetic Ancestry Continuum

link.title: Beyond Discrete Ancestry Groups: Distribution-Aware In-Context Learning for Cancer Outcome Prediction Across the Genetic Ancestry Continuum

entry.content:
Machine learning models for omics-based prediction of cancer outcomes are commonly built on aggregated data without distinguishing ancestry groups, or under an ancestry-discrete design, which partitions samples into ancestry groups and fits a separate model within each group. Recent evidence shows that this approach is inherently limited: predictive accuracy declines with genetic distance from the training samples, even within a single ancestry group, because the data distribution shifts continuously rather than only between predefined categories. In this paper, we propose distribution-aware in-context learning (DA-ICL) for ancestry-continuum modeling. Our method extends conventional ancestry-discrete modeling to ancestry-continuum modeling, capturing the nonstationary omics-endpoint relationship across the genetic continuum while enabling efficient modeling through an in-context learning foundation model. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating the superiority of the ancestry-continuum over ancestry-discrete modeling, along with empirical results supporting the proposed framework. Source code is available at https://github.com/ai4pm/DA-ICL-Continuum.

Read more

entry.title: Beyond Empirical Support: Structured Outlier Generation via Sinkhorn Optimal Transport

link.title: Beyond Empirical Support: Structured Outlier Generation via Sinkhorn Optimal Transport

entry.content:
Outliers are essential for evaluating and improving the robustness of machine learning systems, especially when future distributions may differ significantly from historical training data. In high-stakes applications, robustness often depends on rare cases that finite datasets fail to capture, making simple resampling or perturbation insufficient for stress scenario generation. Existing outlier synthesis methods typically rely on sparse neighborhoods, low support latent regions, or classifier boundary crossings, which can be heuristic, unstable, and tied to specific modalities or architectures. We therefore propose Sinkhorn Boundary Outlier Generation (SBOG), a structured framework for latent-space outlier generation that couples Sinkhorn optimal transport geometry with distributionally robust boundary modeling. The resulting Sinkhorn-induced support cost guides the sampler toward weakly supported boundary regions, while semantic constraints prevent uncontrolled drift from the intended context, yielding controlled deviations from the in-distribution reference measure rather than arbitrary sparse-region samples. Experiments on time series anomaly generation and image outlier synthesis show that our framework produces informative, semantically controlled outliers and improves downstream robustness evaluation across modalities, providing a foundation for stress scenario generation beyond empirical support.

Read more

entry.title: Beyond ICA: Identifiability by Symmetry Breaking

link.title: Beyond ICA: Identifiability by Symmetry Breaking

entry.content:
We prove the population-level identifiability of deep generative models (DGMs) with piecewise-affine (PWA) decoders and Gaussian mixture model (GMM) priors, in a purely unsupervised setting. We introduce three algebraic contrast principles for symmetry breaking: domain contrast, which trivializes the mixture symmetry group, a label-free counterpart of the sufficient-variability assumption of nonlinear ICA; mechanism contrast, which ensures every decoder branch gets an observational boundary across which it toggles alone; and interaction contrast, which forbids parameter conspiracies between latent components and decoder branches. Together they exploit the interplay between the discrete combinatorics of the PWA map and the continuous symmetry structure of the latent GMM. Continuity is replaced by algebraic symmetry conditions; injectivity is decoupled from structural identification and required only for pointwise inversion. Our results form a hierarchy: from law identifiability (LID; latent distribution up to a global affine map) through map identifiability (MID; decoder up to the same map) to posterior and pointwise identifiability. The ICA-form ambiguity emerges under conditions on diagonal component covariances. The interaction contrast is the only one of our contrasts required on the estimator side. To our knowledge this is the first to develop algebraic symmetry-breaking into an identifiability engine for a concrete nonlinear model class, the first to admit discontinuous decoders, and the first to handle fully non-injective decoders, where every observation admits multiple latent codes.

Read more

entry.title: Beyond Prediction Residuals: Conformal Regret Calibration for Robust Contextual Linear Optimization

link.title: Beyond Prediction Residuals: Conformal Regret Calibration for Robust Contextual Linear Optimization

entry.content:
Predict-then-optimize systems convert contextual forecasts into decisions, yet conformal robust optimization typically calibrates prediction residuals rather than downstream loss. For linear optimization, this parameter-space geometry can be badly misaligned with decision risk: large objective perturbations may preserve the optimizer, while small boundary-crossing perturbations may cause substantial regret. We introduce Conformal Regret Sets, a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that conformalizes an optimization-derived regret surrogate and uses its calibrated level set for minimax-regret refinement. We first show that directly conformalizing exact regret, although sufficient to certify the nominal predict-then-optimize decision, yields a degenerate robust problem: absent an exogenous bounded support, every alternative decision has unbounded worst-case regret. We therefore use SPO+, a pointwise upper bound on exact regret, as the conformal score, obtaining distribution-free finite-sample marginal regret guarantees under exchangeability. For contextual linear programs, the resulting set decomposes into polyhedral pieces aligned with the normal fan of the feasible polytope. A vertex is active if and only if its predicted suboptimality gap is at most half the calibrated threshold $\eta$, enabling local, output-sensitive generation of all relevant pieces. Moreover, if $\Gamma$ is the predicted gap to the closest competing vertex, the nominal and refined decisions admit the sharper worst-case-regret certificate $(\eta-2\Gamma)+$, with an exact early exit when $\eta\leq 2\Gamma$. Experiments on contextual fractional knapsack validate the geometry and certificates: continuous refinement reduces the $0.95$-quantile and $\operatorname{CVaR}{0.95}$ of regret by $9.1\%$ and $13.1\%$ relative to nominal PTO, while vertex-restricted refinement changes only $10.0\%$ of nominal decisions.

Read more
