author.name: Peiwen Qiu, Prashant Khanduri, Jia Liu

entry.summary: Bilevel optimization is a fundamental framework for machine learning problems, where an upper-level (UL) objective depends on the solution of a nested lower-level (LL) problem. Existing bilevel algorithms typically assume that the LL objective is available for evaluation, differentiation, or unrolling. However, this assumption can fail when the LL response is produced by a black-box solver, simulator, adversary, or learned predictor. In this paper, we study LL agnostic bilevel optimization, where the UL learner has access only to an approximate LL solution $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ and cannot query the LL objective, its gradients, Hessian/Jacobian information, or the procedure that generates the LL response. We propose LeGo-BiO, a coordinate-wise pseudo-hypergradient method that estimates the missing Jacobian $\nabla _{\mathbf{x}}\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ using finite differences of $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\cdot)$. For each UL coordinate, LeGo-BiO constructs a decision vector subject to 1-sparse updates, thereby isolating the corresponding Jacobian column needed in the UL gradient computation. This avoids the directional-projection limitation of full-parameter response differences and, unlike derivative-free/zeroth-order approximations of the entire UL gradient, preserves the available first-order gradient information with respect to the UL variables for more accurate UL gradient evaluation. We establish convergence guarantees for LeGo-BiO in both deterministic and stochastic settings under an LL error-bound/Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type condition, without requiring LL strong convexity. Our bounds yield an $O(T^{-1})$ rate in the deterministic setting and an $O(T^{-1/2})$ rate in the stochastic setting when the LL approximation error decreases geometrically. Experiments demonstrate competitive performance of LeGo-BiO despite being agnostic to the LL objective.

entry.title: Lyapunov-Based Sample Complexity Analysis for Weakly-Coupled MDPs

link.title: Lyapunov-Based Sample Complexity Analysis for Weakly-Coupled MDPs

entry.content:
We study the sample complexity of learning in average-reward weakly-coupled Markov decision processes (WCMDPs) and Restless Bandits (RBs) under a generative model. Naive reduction to a tabular MDP leads to high complexity bounds as the state-action space is exponentially large in the number of arms $N$. By exploiting the weakly coupled structure, we show that near-optimal policies can be learned with sample and computational complexities that are polynomial in $N$. Specifically, we analyze the plug-in approach, which applies an efficient planning algorithm to an empirical model estimated from data. For fully heterogeneous WCMDPs, we establish the first finite-sample PAC guarantee with polynomial complexity and an $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ optimality gap. For homogeneous RBs, we further prove that a smaller optimality gap is achievable under mild structural assumptions. A primary technical contribution is a novel Lyapunov-based analysis framework. Unlike classical approaches that rely on the difficult-to-control bias function, our framework uses an explicitly constructed Lyapunov function along with a drift transfer technique between the true and empirical models. A key step of independent interest in our framework is a fine-grained perturbation analysis for the underlying linear programming (LP) relaxation, which provides a general tool for analyzing LP-based policies and weakly-coupled systems.

Read more

entry.title: MML Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis

link.title: MML Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis

entry.content:
Principal component analysis (PCA) is perhaps the most widely used method for data dimensionality reduction. A key question in PCA is deciding how many components to retain. This manuscript describes a new approach to automatically selecting the number of principal components based on the Bayesian minimum message length method of inductive inference. We derive new estimates of the isotropic residual variance and loadings, and establish their bias and asymptotic distributions. For moderate latent dimensions, the residual variance estimate improves on maximum likelihood, and the implied eigenvalue shrinkage approaches the Stein-optimal shrinkage for strong signals.

Read more

entry.title: Mamba Can Learn Low-Dimensional Targets In-Context via Test-Time Feature Learning

link.title: Mamba Can Learn Low-Dimensional Targets In-Context via Test-Time Feature Learning

entry.content:
Mamba, a recently proposed linear-time sequence model, has attracted significant attention for its computational efficiency and strong empirical performance. However, a rigorous theoretical understanding of its underlying mechanisms remains limited. In this work, we provide a theoretical analysis of Mamba’s in-context learning (ICL) capability by focusing on tasks defined by low-dimensional nonlinear target functions. Specifically, we study in-context learning of a single-index model $y \approx g_*(\langle \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{x} \rangle)$, which depends on only a single relevant direction $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, referred to as feature. We prove that Mamba, pretrained by gradient-based methods, can achieve efficient ICL via test-time feature learning, extracting the relevant direction directly from context examples. Consequently, we establish a test-time sample complexity that improves upon linear Transformers – analyzed to behave like kernel methods – and is comparable to nonlinear Transformers, which have been shown to surpass the Correlational Statistical Query (CSQ) lower bound and achieve near information-theoretically optimal rate in previous works. Our analysis reveals the crucial role of the nonlinear gating mechanism in Mamba for feature extraction, highlighting it as the fundamental driver behind Mamba’s ability to achieve both computational efficiency and high performance.

Read more

entry.title: Massively Parallel Exact Inference for Hawkes Processes

link.title: Massively Parallel Exact Inference for Hawkes Processes

entry.content:
Multivariate Hawkes processes are a widely used class of self-exciting point processes, but maximum likelihood estimation naively scales as $O(N^2)$ in the number of events. The canonical linear exponential Hawkes process admits a faster $O(N)$ recurrence, but prior work evaluates this recurrence sequentially, without exploiting parallelization on modern GPUs. We show that the Hawkes process intensity can be expressed as a product of sparse transition matrices admitting a linear-time associative multiply, enabling computation via a parallel prefix scan. This yields a massively parallelizable algorithm for estimation of linear exponential Hawkes processes. Our method reduces the computational complexity to approximately $O(N/P)$ with $P$ parallel processors, and naturally yields a batching scheme to maintain constant memory usage, avoiding GPU memory constraints. Importantly, it computes the exact likelihood without any additional assumptions or approximations, preserving the simplicity and interpretability of the model. We demonstrate orders-of-magnitude speedups on simulated and real datasets, scaling to thousands of nodes and tens of millions of events, substantially beyond scales reported in prior work. We provide an open-source PyTorch library implementing our optimizations.

Read more

entry.title: Matchability-Aware Conformal Prediction for Open-Ended Language Model Generation

link.title: Matchability-Aware Conformal Prediction for Open-Ended Language Model Generation

entry.content:
Large language models (LLMs) often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers. We propose CAELUM, a framework that builds semantic prediction sets while separating aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. CAELUM samples answers using an ensemble of clarification prompts, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and estimates the aleatoric and epistemic components via kernel-based von Neumann entropy before calibrating nonconformity scores with split conformal prediction. We use a weight $w_\lambda(x)=1+U_{\mathrm{ale}}(x)+\lambda\,U_{\mathrm{epi}}(x)$ to control for the contribution of the epistemic uncertainty of each instance and fit a coefficient $\lambda^\star$ to minimize prediction set size. When the objective is nonflat and selection is stable across splits, $\lambda^\star$ could be a diagnostic, where large values may indicate epistemic dominance (retrieve, abstain) and $\lambda^\star\to 0$ aleatoric dominance (clarify). For individual queries, a log ratio $R(x)$ compares the weighted epistemic component with the aleatoric component. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the coverage is capped by matchability, the fraction of items whose reference answer appears in any sampled cluster. Empirically, this matchability can be predicted from the original question features using a lightweight classifier. We use those predictions to define a stratum and derive a conformal coverage bound within it. Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations (4-32B), mean coverage is 0.74 in the learned stratum versus 0.65 overall, averaged over the 78 evaluations using the learned classifier. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/caelum/

Read more

entry.title: Match the Geometry Before the Surrogate: Extreme Low-Budget Optimization in High Dimensions

link.title: Match the Geometry Before the Surrogate: Extreme Low-Budget Optimization in High Dimensions

entry.content:
Low-budget molecular optimization is often framed as Bayesian optimization in a learned latent space, but standard benchmarks typically allow hundreds or thousands of evaluations, whereas a realistic wet-lab round may allow only a few dozen. We revisit this regime using a SELFIES molecular variational autoencoder (VAE) with a Gaussian prior and GuacaMol objectives at N = 30 evaluations. The main finding is not a new surrogate model, but an interaction in candidate generation. The encoder means of a reference set of molecules concentrate near a narrow spherical shell, while many high-dimensional optimizers propose candidates from boxes or box-shaped trust regions. We study a simple constraint, the on-sphere scaffold, that restricts candidate generation to this shell. We then introduce two minimal optimizers to probe what remains useful once the support is fixed. GeoWalk performs geodesic local search on the shell without a surrogate. After 30 evaluations, it shows no detected difference from a Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate on the shell, which is ahead earlier in the budget. GeoCMA adds covariance learning in a random subspace. It does not improve on GeoWalk in the molecular benchmark. On LassoBench it has a lower mean loss than GeoWalk, but full-dimensional CMA-ES remains stronger on most tasks. A factorial experiment with a single GP crosses the candidate support (shell or box) with the acquisition maximizer (a finite candidate set or a continuous optimizer). In this benchmark, shell candidates outperformed box candidates when acquisition was maximized over a candidate set, but not with continuous maximization by L-BFGS-B. These results come from a controlled study of one Gaussian-prior VAE benchmark and do not recommend VAEs for molecular optimization. The practical lesson is to control the candidate support and the acquisition maximizer before attributing a gain to the surrogate.

Read more

entry.title: Maximin Robust Bayesian Experimental Design

link.title: Maximin Robust Bayesian Experimental Design

entry.content:
We address the brittleness of Bayesian experimental design under model misspecification by formulating the problem as a max–min game between the experimenter and an adversarial nature subject to information-theoretic constraints. We demonstrate that this approach yields a robust objective governed by Sibson’s $\alpha$-mutual information~(MI), which identifies the $\alpha$-tilted posterior as the robust belief update and establishes the R'enyi divergence as the appropriate measure of conditional information gain. To mitigate the bias and variance of nested Monte Carlo estimators needed to estimate Sibson’s $\alpha$-MI, we adopt a PAC-Bayes framework to search over stochastic design policies, yielding rigorous high-probability lower bounds on the robust expected information gain that explicitly control finite-sample error.

Read more

entry.title: Measuring Public Institutions and their Agents: Disparities and Agreement, with Application to Asylum Decisions in the U.S. Immigration Courts

link.title: Measuring Public Institutions and their Agents: Disparities and Agreement, with Application to Asylum Decisions in the U.S. Immigration Courts

entry.content:
Public institutions derive their legitimacy from the professionalism and impartiality of their agents. In order to maintain standards of conduct, the performance of an agent is often compared to the performance of her peers. But public institutions typically assign agents to different tasks, and as a result, naive comparisons may reflect the difficulty of the assignment and not an agent’s performance. To address this concern, we develop measures of disparity and agreement that compare an agent’s performance with the potential performance of randomly selected peers who could have been assigned the same set of tasks. We then give realistic conditions under which disparity is identified from the marginal distribution of each agent’s actions. We also show how agreement, which is generally unidentified when agents are assigned to different tasks, can be bounded or estimated under sensitivity assumptions about the dependence between potential outcomes. Finally, we use a nonparametric Bayesian model to examine applications for asylum filed between 2007 and 2014 in the widely studied and often maligned U.S. immigration courts. Our results do not support the picture of widespread partiality asserted in previous empirical work. At both the judge and court level, we find limited disparity and substantial potential agreement.

Read more

entry.title: Mechanistic Interpretability with Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators

link.title: Mechanistic Interpretability with Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators

entry.content:
We introduce sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs), a new class of sparse autoencoders that operate in function spaces rather than fixed-dimensional Euclidean representations. We formalize the functional representation hypothesis, where data are explained through sparse compositions of structured functions. Unlike standard SAEs that represent concepts with scalar activations, SAE-NOs parameterize concepts as functions, enabling representations that capture not only a concept’s presence, but also how and where it is expressed across the input domain. We achieve this through joint sparsity: concept sparsity selects active concepts, while domain sparsity governs where they are expressed. We instantiate this framework using Fourier neural operators (SAE-FNOs), parameterizing concepts as integral operators in the Fourier domain. This functional and spectral parameterization is particularly advantageous when data exhibit spatial structure across scales or when concepts are frequency-structured. We characterize SAE-FNO on vision data and demonstrate that it learns localized patterns, uses concepts more efficiently, and exhibits stable concept characteristics across sparsity levels. We further show that SAE-FNO adapts to changes in domain size and generalizes across discretizations, operating at resolutions beyond those seen during training, where standard SAEs fail. We also introduce lifting into SAEs and show theoretically and empirically that it acts as a preconditioner that accelerates optimization. Overall, our results show that moving from vector-valued to functional parameterizations, with concept and domain sparsity, extends SAEs from representing concept presence to modeling structured concept expression, highlighting the importance of parameterization.

Read more

entry.title: Metropolis-Adjusted Diffusion Models

link.title: Metropolis-Adjusted Diffusion Models

entry.content:
Sampling from score-based diffusion models incurs bias due to both time discretisation and the approximation of the score function. A common strategy for reducing this bias is to apply corrector steps based on the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) at each noise level within a predictor-corrector framework. However, ULA is itself a \emph{biased} sampler, as it discretises a continuous diffusion process. In this work, we consider \emph{adjusted} Langevin correctors that employ Metropolis–Hastings (MH) or Barker’s accept-reject steps to correct for this bias. Since the target density ratio typically required by MH-based algorithms is unavailable, we propose methods that instead utilise the score function to compute the correct acceptance probability. We introduce the first exact method for adjusting Langevin corrections in diffusion models, based on a two-coin Bernoulli factory algorithm. We also propose an efficient approximation based on Simpson’s rule that achieves accuracy of order $5/2$ in the step size at near-zero marginal cost. We demonstrate that these procedures improve sample quality on both synthetic and image datasets, yielding consistent gains in Fr'echet Inception Distance (FID) on the latter.

Read more

entry.title: Minimax Optimal Early-Stopped Gradient Descent for Gaussian Mixture Classification

link.title: Minimax Optimal Early-Stopped Gradient Descent for Gaussian Mixture Classification

entry.content:
In overparameterised classification, training data can be linearly separable even when the underlying distribution is not. In this setting, gradient descent (GD) on the logistic loss diverges in norm while converging in direction to a max-margin interpolating classifier, whose implicit bias can be statistically suboptimal. In this work, we show that early stopping can overcome this suboptimality: in a Gaussian mixture model with label-flipping noise, GD stopped at an appropriate oracle time achieves minimax-optimal excess zero-one risk for covariance spectra with fast and continuous decay, including polynomial and exponential spectral decays. Our analysis combines a sharp upper bound for the early-stopped iterate with a matching statistical lower bound over arbitrary classifiers, yielding optimal rates that are validated by experiments. A central technical contribution is a new calibration result that converts excess logistic risk into excess zero-one risk; it handles the model misspecification induced by the label-flipping noise, and removes the square-root rate in standard bounds. We also establish a lower bound for linear interpolators, showing that interpolation can require exponentially more samples than early stopping to achieve the same excess risk.

Read more

entry.title: Minimax Rates and Spectral Distillation for Tree Ensembles

link.title: Minimax Rates and Spectral Distillation for Tree Ensembles

entry.content:
Tree ensembles such as random forests (RFs) and gradient boosting machines (GBMs) are among the most widely used supervised learners, yet their theoretical properties remain incompletely understood. We adopt a spectral perspective on these algorithms, with two main contributions. First, we derive minimax-optimal convergence for RF regression, showing that, under mild regularity conditions on tree growth, the eigenvalue decay of the induced kernel operator governs the statistical rate. Second, we exploit this spectral viewpoint to develop compression schemes for tree ensembles. For RFs, leading eigenfunctions of the kernel operator capture the dominant predictive directions; for GBMs, leading singular vectors of the smoother matrix play an analogous role. Learning nonlinear maps for these spectral representations yields distilled models that are orders of magnitude smaller than the originals while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Our methods compare favorably to state of the art algorithms for forest pruning and rule extraction, with applications to resource constrained computing.

Read more

entry.title: Minimax Regret for Sobolev Kernel-Based Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Minimax Regret for Sobolev Kernel-Based Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
We study the minimax regret rate for episodic kernel-based reinforcement learning, where the expected reward and transition density belong to a Sobolev reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), with continuous state and action spaces, and adversarial initial states. For Sobolev smoothness parameter $ u>0$, state dimension $d_S$, and action dimension $d_A$, we prove that the minimax expected regret over $T$ episodes is $\widetilde\Theta(T^{\max{e_A,e_B}})$, where $e_A= rac{ u+d_A}{2 u+d_A}$, $e_B= rac{ u+d_A+3d_S/2}{2 u+d_A+2d_S}$ with the other model parameters fixed. The two exponents reflect the distinct difficulties of action selection and learning across states. We introduce Sobolev Optimal Value Iteration ( exttt{SOVI}), which attains this rate from observed rewards and transitions. For fixed smoothness and reference-kernel lengthscale, its regret bound has a prefactor polynomial in the state-action dimension $d=d_S+d_A$, horizon $H$, reward and transition RKHS norm bounds $B_r,B_p$, and the norm-comparison factor $\Lambda$, up to logarithmic factors; $\Lambda=1$ for normalized Mat'ern kernels. The algorithm separates initial action selection from continuation-value estimation and combines local polynomial approximation with the shared RKHS structure of the approximation errors. Our matching upper and lower bounds determine the optimal dependence on the number of episodes for Sobolev kernel-based reinforcement learning regret minimization. Thus, we partially address the open problem in Vakili(2024) under Sobolev kernel RL.

entry.title: Model-assisted semi-supervised estimation of the Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring

link.title: Model-assisted semi-supervised estimation of the Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring

entry.content:
We study semi-supervised estimation of the full-lifetime Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring using finite covariate-only samples from two populations. A model-assisted estimator is constructed by adjusting censored pair comparisons with differences between labeled and auxiliary feature means. Resource weights minimize first-order variance within the working projection class. Under joint independent censoring and regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality through a four-pool influence representation that accounts for censoring distributions estimated from the same labeled records. Consistent variance estimation from all four sample pools yields Wald confidence intervals. The efficiency analysis relates variance reduction to projected comparison signals and auxiliary sample sizes and characterizes the gap to the semiparametric bound. A fixed-horizon extension accommodates half-weighted ties and the terminal mass induced by capping follow-up. Simulations show increasing precision gains with auxiliary sample size under moderate or strong projected signals, with finite-sample losses in some settings with zero or weak projected signals. A five-year Rotterdam breast-cancer comparison illustrates precision gains and variability across label allocations when auxiliary samples are formed by controlled outcome withholding.

Read more

entry.title: Modeling inter-exceedance times of extreme heat days

link.title: Modeling inter-exceedance times of extreme heat days

entry.content:
Extreme heat days, here defined as exceedances of a local calendar-day-based 95% quantile, often occur in clusters forming multi-day heatwaves. A calendar-day based threshold allows for the detection of temperature extremes across all seasons, which may impact several economic sectors, public health and ecosystems. Previous approaches to modeling the occurrences of extreme heat events typically treat heat event duration and the time between heat events separately. We propose modeling the inter-exceedance times (IETs) between extreme heat days, allowing for a unified description within a single model. We consider several candidate distributions for the IETs of extreme heat days and find that the zero-inflated discrete Weibull (ZIDW) distribution clearly provides the best fit according to Pearson’s chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests. The ZIDW distribution is a flexible model for count data exhibiting excess zeros as well as over- and under-dispersion: the zero-inflation component captures the pronounced clustering of heat days, while the discrete Weibull component adequately accounts for over-dispersion. Heat days are extracted using both trend-adjusted and non-trend-adjusted thresholds. This allows the analysis of general changes in the occurrence of extreme heat days as well as changes after accounting for the general increase in temperature.

entry.title: Modeling the Joint Distribution of Box Score Statistics: A Gaussian Copula Approach

link.title: Modeling the Joint Distribution of Box Score Statistics: A Gaussian Copula Approach

entry.content:
What is the probability that LeBron James records at least 27 points, 7 rebounds, and 7 assists tonight? While an interesting statistical question by itself, the rise of sports betting and multi-leg parlays has made answering this question increasingly relevant. However, coming up with an estimated likelihood is tricky, since box score statistics aren’t independent. We estimate the joint probability that a player reaches a combination of thresholds in points, assists, and rebounds using a Gaussian copula, fit separately for each player using only their previous games. We compare it with two benchmarks: the product of the empirical marginal probabilities (i.e. assuming independence) and the empirical frequency of the joint event. Across ~22,000 player-observations, the Gaussian copula performs on par or better than either benchmark at lower threshold levels, with large gains at high joint exceedance levels. Because it is generative, the model also allows for probabilistic calculations for combinations that a player has rarely or never produced.

Read more

entry.title: Multilevel and Sequential Monte Carlo for Training-Free Diffusion Guidance

link.title: Multilevel and Sequential Monte Carlo for Training-Free Diffusion Guidance

entry.content:
We address the problem of accurate, training-free guidance for conditional generation in trained diffusion models. Existing methods typically rely on point-estimates to approximate the posterior score, often resulting in biased approximations that fail to capture multimodality inherent to the reverse process of diffusion models. We propose a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) framework that integrates over the full denoising distribution to construct an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of $p_\theta(y\mid x_t)$, avoiding the bias of existing training-free guidance methods. To ensure computational tractability, we incorporate variance-reduction schemes based on MultiLevel Monte Carlo (MLMC). We evaluate on three image generation tasks. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classifier guidance, our approach improves accuracy by 18 and 38 points respectively over the strongest training-free baseline. On CelebA-HQ joint-attribute guidance, three existing methods (DPS, LGD, TFG) used within our framework all outperform the closest SMC-based comparator (TDS) by 25-37 points, and improve over the strongest baseline by 2-14 points.

Read more

entry.title: Multiple change-point detection via bottom-up scanning

link.title: Multiple change-point detection via bottom-up scanning

entry.content:
We study nonparametric multiple change-point detection for high-dimensional sequences, aiming to identify time points at which the underlying distribution changes. While many existing methods perform well when change-points are well-separated, their performance can deteriorate when structural breaks are densely clustered. To address this challenge, we propose gBottomup, a graph-based bottom-up framework for multiple change-point detection in high-dimensional settings. gBottomup constructs a hierarchical segmentation by proposing merges of adjacent segments and verifying them through an unmerge rule that combines absolute significance with relative local heterogeneity, thereby adaptively refining partitions and estimating the number of change-points. Simulation results demonstrate that gBottomup performs reliably across a range of structural configurations and is particularly effective in frequent change-point settings, where existing top-down procedures may lose sensitivity. We illustrate the proposed method through an analysis of high-dimensional sensor data from an experimental hydraulic system.

Read more

entry.title: Multistage Defer Trees for Hybrid Interpretability: If at First You Can’t Succeed, Tree Again

link.title: Multistage Defer Trees for Hybrid Interpretability: If at First You Can’t Succeed, Tree Again

entry.content:
Recent work has shown that well-optimized individual decision trees can match complex black box models in some settings, primarily in noisy domains. For the remaining settings, however, complex ensembled compositions of trees often achieve higher accuracy at the cost of interpretability, leaving practitioners with difficult modeling decisions along an accuracy-interpretability tradeoff. Ideally, we would like to classify as much of the data as possible with one or a small number of trees, achieving interpretability for most samples while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy. We introduce Multistage Defer Trees: a sequence of sparse decision trees that each make predictions for most samples, while deferring a small proportion to the next tree in the sequence or, ultimately, to a black box. We demonstrate that we can train this model class to match the performance of complex tree-based ensembles while routing most samples through only one or a small number of sparse decision trees. We discuss a range of techniques for training these models while maintaining simplicity. Our method expands the accuracy–interpretability frontier in settings where single-tree methods remain insufficient, demonstrating that even when complex models are necessary, they need not be fully opaque.

Read more

entry.title: Near-Purity Screening and Dominant-Atom Estimation in Softmax Mixtures and Their Ensembles

link.title: Near-Purity Screening and Dominant-Atom Estimation in Softmax Mixtures and Their Ensembles

entry.content:
We study near-purity screening and dominant-atom estimation in softmax mixtures, whose components share a common set of category features. A mixture is called $\varepsilon$-pure if one of its mixing weights is at least $1-\varepsilon$. We introduce the Trace of Latent Covariance Criterion ($\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$), a direct estimator of the trace of the covariance matrix of the latent mixing measure, constructed without estimating its atoms or weights, or knowing the number of components. Unlike existing moment-based approaches, our estimator is constructed for the softmax family and does not require knowledge or estimation of the feature distribution. We establish finite-sample guarantees for $\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$, showing that it achieves a parametric convergence rate up to an additive approximation error of order $p^{-1/2}$, without requiring minimum separation between mixture atoms. We also study estimation of the dominant atom in near-pure mixtures by fitting a single softmax component. We prove that the resulting maximum likelihood estimator has an error bound consisting of the usual parametric term and a bias term governed by the weighted distances between the dominant and remaining atoms, revealing adaptation to the geometry of the mixture. Finally, we extend near-purity screening and dominant-atom estimation to ensembles of softmax mixtures with shared atoms and mixture-specific weights. We apply $\mathrm{TLC}^{2}$ separately to each ensemble member to screen for near-purity without knowing the number of components. Under additional assumptions, clustering the resulting dominant-atom estimators yields finite-sample guarantees for estimating the shared atoms. An application to the Million Song Dataset illustrates how the estimated softmax directions reveal interpretable structure in the data.

entry.title: Nearest-Neighbor Radii under Dependent Sampling

link.title: Nearest-Neighbor Radii under Dependent Sampling

entry.content:
Nearest-neighbor methods are fundamental to classical and modern machine learning, yet their geometric properties are typically analyzed under independent sampling. In this paper, we study the nearest-neighbor radii under dependent sampling. We consider strong mixing dependent observations and ask whether dependence changes the scale of nearest-neighbor neighborhoods. We establish distribution-free almost sure convergence under polynomial mixing and sharp non-asymptotic moment bounds under geometric mixing. The moment bounds depend on the local intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient dimension, making the results applicable to high-dimensional data supported on lower-dimensional manifolds. Synthetic experiments and real-world time-series benchmarks illustrate the theory, showing that nearest-neighbor geometry remains informative under dependent sampling.

entry.title: Network Reconstruction via Jeffreys Prior under Missing Sufficient Statistics

link.title: Network Reconstruction via Jeffreys Prior under Missing Sufficient Statistics

entry.content:
Methods for the reconstruction of economic networks from aggregate information are important for modeling, analysis and policymaking. The traditional Fitness Model (FM) achieves good performance by using node-specific variables that are easily accessible (e.g., GDP for countries or total assets for banks or firms) and the overall link density as the only sufficient statistics. However, it often ignores additional contextual or mesoscopic features which may be more difficult to observe. Here we extend the framework by incorporating block structure as in the Fitness-Corrected Block Model (FCBM), which allows for heterogeneous densities within and across blocks, but in the deliberately more challenging setting where such block-specific densities are not empirically available. Our method uses a Jeffreys prior to provide an unbiased distribution of all compatible solutions and associated entropies, that are otherwise left unidentified, and selects a single reconstruction at the median of this entropy distribution to compensate for the missing sufficient statistics. We evaluate the procedure on nine international-trade networks using GDP as node fitness and World Bank regions as an externally specified partition. The method systematically outperforms the baseline Block-Agnostic FM (which uses the same observed network input statistic) and sometimes even the FCBM (which always uses more information). Controlled synthetic networks confirm that the median is the best of four entropy-based representatives for a range of densities and regional effects similar to the empirical ones, while other representatives can perform better when parameters are pushed far from their realistic range. Overall, our method compensates for missing sufficient statistics via a median-entropy estimate that is empirically very robust within a realistic range of parameters.

Read more

entry.title: No Universal Winner in Model Selection: Regression versus Representational Similarity Analysis

link.title: No Universal Winner in Model Selection: Regression versus Representational Similarity Analysis

entry.content:
Selecting among competing computational models is central to cognitive psychology and neuroscience, yet the relative model-selection performance of regression and representational similarity analysis (RSA) remains unclear. We compared these approaches using Monte Carlo simulations and empirical data. Univariate simulations compared generating and rival feature models against the same response under direct-linear and geometry-based mappings. Under direct-linear generation, regression outperformed correlation-distance RSA/Spearman but not RSA/Pearson. Under geometry-linear generation, neither approach showed a significant advantage, whereas correlation-distance RSA outperformed regression under a sigmoid readout, although this advantage did not extend to Euclidean-distance RSA. Feature dimensionality, covariance, and PCA preprocessing further influenced model-selection accuracy. In multivoxel simulations, pattern component modeling (PCM) showed superior performance under spatially correlated noise, while crossnobis improved selection relative to squared Euclidean RSA under the same condition. Feature reweighting improved held-out representational correspondence for both generating and rival models without consistently improving model selection. Separate signal-strength comparisons yielded different method rankings. In empirical data from 4,026 words, all methods preferred frequency over affect features, but small-sample preference stability depended on distance measures and preprocessing. Together, these findings demonstrate that model-selection performance depends on stimulus-response mappings, representational geometry, measurement noise, and inferential objectives.

entry.title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization

link.title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization

entry.content:
We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

entry.title: Numerical and analytical strategies to propagate correlated uncertainties through the discrete Fourier transform

link.title: Numerical and analytical strategies to propagate correlated uncertainties through the discrete Fourier transform

entry.content:
The Fourier transform underpins a range of comparisons between atomistic simulations and scattering measurements, yet uncertainty propagation through it is seldom discussed, and correlations between data points are usually ignored. Here, we give a pedagogical account of uncertainty propagation through the discrete Fourier transform, including the full covariance matrix. Two routes are described: a numerical scheme that samples from the multivariate normal distribution describing the data, and an analytical scheme that treats the transform as a change of basis. We discuss the scaling behaviour of these methods and demonstrate their utility on problems that link simulation to scattering: the Faber–Ziman partial structure factors of liquid water, and the dynamic structure factor obtained from a rotational autocorrelation function.

Read more

entry.title: Objective Diversification of Dynamic Hedging

link.title: Objective Diversification of Dynamic Hedging

entry.content:
A hedging objective reflects the risk preference of the hedger, so the conventional approach is to estimate the hedge ratio directly under the chosen objective. This paper asks whether that estimate should be used alone. We construct five objective-specific rolling hedge-ratio estimators—minimum variance, least absolute deviation (LAD), downside semivariance, lower-tail quantile, and Expected Shortfall (ES)—from the same historical stock–market returns, and combine the resulting estimates under a fixed final evaluation objective. Separate multi-output ExtraTrees models predict the within-stock-date ranks of the five candidates under MSE, LAD, downside semivariance, and 10\% quantile loss. The design uses pre-specified 60-, 90-, 120-, and 180-day windows with objective-matched rolling estimators as benchmarks. Adaptive weighting improves the corresponding loss in all sixteen objective–window comparisons. Equal weighting, which uses the same objective-specific hedge ratios without state variables or learned reweighting, already improves downside and quantile hedging. The results therefore suggest that estimates generated under other objectives can be useful even when the final hedging preference and evaluation objective are fixed, while adaptive weighting can provide a further improvement.

Read more

entry.title: Odds-Structured Distributional Regression for Interpretable Time-to-Event Prediction

link.title: Odds-Structured Distributional Regression for Interpretable Time-to-Event Prediction

entry.content:
Time-to-event prediction is fundamentally challenged by partial observability and aleatoric uncertainty. In clinical medicine, for instance, the timing of disease progression or acute readmission is contingent on highly dynamic and largely latent health trajectories. Rather than forcing a deterministic point forecast, distributional regression offers a principled means to address this complexity by predicting a probability distribution over time. However, explaining these distributional predictions presents a key obstacle: raw distribution parameters output by the model are abstract mathematical quantities that do not align well with domain concepts. To gain interpretability, we propose a novel paradigm where output parameters are designed to be additive in log-odds—a widely established measure in clinical risk modeling. Our approach, called ODDS-DR, moves beyond technical convenience to deliver clear domain alignment as well as the layer-wise computational structure required for robust, time-dependent feature attribution. Validated across two real-world clinical cohorts, our framework matches state-of-the-art predictive performance while resolving distributional outputs into interpretable risk markers across flexible prognostic horizons.

Read more

entry.title: On Generalization in Bilevel Least Squares with Overparameterized Neural Networks

link.title: On Generalization in Bilevel Least Squares with Overparameterized Neural Networks

entry.content:
Bilevel optimization addresses machine learning problems in which the outer objective is a value function implicitly defined through the solution of an inner problem. While its algorithmic aspects are well developed, its generalization properties remain much less understood. In this paper, we study the generalization of inexact gradient methods when both objectives are least-squares regression problems and when the estimator of the value function’s gradient, or hypergradient, is obtained by implicit differentiation in function space. This approach allows us to derive stationarity bounds for these methods in terms of the uniform generalization errors of the two regression functions needed to estimate the hypergradient. When these regression functions are defined as overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient flow with early stopping, we obtain explicit finite-sample bounds on these generalization errors in the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime. Combining these with our general inexact gradient analysis shows the effect of sample size on the overall convergence of the bilevel method. Numerical experiments on synthetic data illustrate our results. Beyond the NTK regime, further experiments reveal an initialization-dependent implicit bias induced by the bilevel structure, which can lead to feature learning at the inner level and overall performance improvements.

Read more

entry.title: Online Learning on Hidden-Convex Losses via Algorithmic Equivalence: Optimal Regret, Geometric Barrier, and Bandit Feedback

link.title: Online Learning on Hidden-Convex Losses via Algorithmic Equivalence: Optimal Regret, Geometric Barrier, and Bandit Feedback

entry.content:
We study adversarial online learning with hidden-convex losses, i.e., nonconvex losses that become convex after a nonlinear reparameterization. Ghai, Lu and Hazan (2022) proved that, under geometric and smoothness assumptions, online gradient descent (OGD) on such nonconvex losses approximately simulates online mirror descent (OMD) on the underlying convex losses with a suitable regularizer, yielding $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ regret. They left open whether the optimal $\Theta(\sqrt{T})$ regret from online convex optimization can be recovered in this hidden-convex setting. We answer this question affirmatively. More specifically, via a sharper discrete-time algorithmic equivalence argument, we prove that OGD achieves $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret under the same assumptions, matching the optimal worst-case rate for adversarial online convex optimization. We also address another open question of Ghai, Lu and Hazan (2022) by clarifying the geometry required for this algorithmic equivalence. We replace the diagonal-Jacobian sufficient condition with a necessary-and-sufficient Hessian compatibility condition, thereby expanding the class of admissible reparameterizations. We complement our tight regret bound with a lower bound showing that OGD suffers $\Omega(T)$ regret even with a stepsize of order $1/\sqrt{T}$, for a smooth Hessian incompatible reparameterization between convex domains and an adversarial sequence of hidden-convex losses. Finally, we extend our analysis to one-point bandit feedback and prove a $\mathcal{O}(T^{3/4})$ expected regret bound for bandit OGD with spherical smoothing, matching its classical rate on convex losses.

entry.title: Online Multivariate Regularized Distributional Regression for High-dimensional Probabilistic Electricity Price Forecasting

link.title: Online Multivariate Regularized Distributional Regression for High-dimensional Probabilistic Electricity Price Forecasting

entry.content:
Probabilistic electricity price forecasting (PEPF) is vital for short-term electricity markets, yet the multivariate nature of day-ahead prices - spanning 24 consecutive hours - remains underexplored. At the same time, real-time decision-making requires methods that are both accurate and fast. We introduce an online algorithm for multivariate distributional regression models, allowing efficient modeling of the conditional means, variances, and dependence structures of electricity prices. The approach combines multivariate distributional regression with online coordinate descent and LASSO-type regularization (absolute shrinkage and selection operator), enabling scalable estimation in high-dimensional covariate spaces. Additionally, we propose a regularized estimation path over increasingly complex dependence structures, allowing for early stopping and avoiding overfitting. In a case study using historical data from the German day-ahead market, the proposed method yields interpretable and well-calibrated joint prediction intervals for the 24-dimensional price distribution and provides robust performance across a range of proper scoring rules. The results underscore the importance of modeling the dependence structure of electricity prices. Furthermore, we analyze the trade-off between predictive accuracy and computational costs for batch and online estimation and provide a high-performing open-source Python implementation in the ondil package.

Read more

entry.title: On the Burden of Achieving Fairness in Conformal Prediction

link.title: On the Burden of Achieving Fairness in Conformal Prediction

entry.content:
Conformal prediction is often calibrated with a single pooled threshold, but this can hide cross-group heterogeneity in score distributions and distort group-wise coverage. We study this phenomenon through the population score distributions underlying split conformal calibration. First, we derive a conservation law and lower bound showing that pooled calibration incurs irreducible group-wise coverage distortion at a scale set by cross-group quantile heterogeneity. Second, we demonstrate that the two leading fairness definitions for conformal prediction, Equalized Coverage and Equalized Set Size, are fundamentally in tension. Third, we quantify the cost of moving between policies which treat groups separately or pool them. Experiments on synthetic and real data confirm the same bidirectional trade-off after finite-sample calibration. Our results show that, for the policy families studied here, calibration choice does not remove cross-group heterogeneity; it determines whether the resulting distortion appears in the coverage or size dimension, providing a principled lens for analyzing fairness-oriented calibration choices in practice.

Read more

entry.title: On the (In)Compatibility between Group Fairness and Individual Fairness

link.title: On the (In)Compatibility between Group Fairness and Individual Fairness

entry.content:
We study the compatibility between utility-optimized statistical parity and individual fairness. While individual fairness seeks to treat similar individuals similarly, optimal statistical parity aims to provide similar treatment to individuals who share relative similarity within their respective sensitive groups. Although both fairness perspectives are desirable, they often conflict in practical applications. Our goal in this work is to analyze the existence of this conflict and its potential solution. In particular, we establish sufficient (sharp) conditions for the compatibility between the optimal (post-processing) statistical parity $L^2$ learning and the ($K$-Lipschitz or $(\epsilon,\delta)$) individual fairness requirements. When a conflict arises, we first relax the optimal statistical parity solution to the Pareto frontier, representing the optimal trade-off between $L^2$ error and statistical disparity, and then examine its compatibility with individual fairness. Our analysis identifies regions along the Pareto frontier that satisfy individual fairness constraints. Additionally, we provide individual fairness guarantees for the composition of a trained model with the optimal post-processing step, enabling practitioners to assess the compatibility of post-processed models. This provides practitioners with a principled approach to achieving Pareto-optimal statistical parity while maintaining individual fairness constraints.

Read more

entry.title: On the robustness of locally D-optimal designs under parameter uncertainty in single-factor generalized linear models

link.title: On the robustness of locally D-optimal designs under parameter uncertainty in single-factor generalized linear models

entry.content:
Local and Bayesian approaches to optimal experimental design specify information about the regression parameters through a nominal value and a prior distribution, respectively. A practical question is whether accounting for parameter uncertainty justifies replacing a locally optimal design. We investigate when locally D-optimal designs remain Bayesian D-optimal in single-factor Poisson, gamma and logistic regression on the unit interval. Analytical arguments and numerical comparisons under normal and uniform slope priors examine how prior form and dispersion affect the optimal support and the Bayesian D-efficiency of retaining a local design.

entry.title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion

link.title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion

entry.content:
Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms is paramount for advancing model training and inference in a principled way. Here, we demonstrate that deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal geometric structure invariant to data modalities and diffusion model implementations. This structure can be largely explained by an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.

Read more

entry.title: Optimal Radial Weighting for Robust Mutual Fund Selection

link.title: Optimal Radial Weighting for Robust Mutual Fund Selection

entry.content:
Identifying skilled mutual funds requires methods that distinguish positive alphas from sampling variation when many funds are evaluated simultaneously. Heavy-tailed returns and dependence across funds complicate this task. We propose a robust selection procedure based on radially weighted alpha estimation in linear factor pricing models. The method uses both the directions and lengths of standardized residuals, estimates marginal scales from pairwise residual differences, and accounts for the estimation of factor loadings. Within the proposed class, inverse-norm weighting minimizes the asymptotic variance of the alpha estimators and maximizes the local asymptotic power of individual tests at a common significance level. For radial weights fixed conditional on the factor design, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control under elliptically symmetric errors and show that the proportion of sufficiently strong positive-alpha funds selected tends to one. The theory accommodates comparable cross-sectional and time-series dimensions and nonvanishing alphas. We also develop a smoothed implementation and assess its finite-sample properties. Simulations show higher true discovery proportions than least-squares and spatial-sign methods under heavy-tailed distributions and improved numerical stability from smoothing. An application to U.S. equity mutual funds examines the subsequent performance of portfolios formed from the selected funds.

Read more

entry.title: Optimal Rates for Adaptive Private $k$-PCA

link.title: Optimal Rates for Adaptive Private $k$-PCA

entry.content:
Given $n$ i.i.d. random matrices $A_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ with common expectation $\Sigma$, the goal of \emph{Differentially Private Stochastic PCA} is to identify a $k$-dimensional subspace capturing the leading variance directions of $\Sigma$, while preserving differential privacy~(DP) for each individual sample $A_i$. \citet{dungler2025iterative} introduced \kdppca, the first algorithm to simultaneously (1) achieve sample complexity $n=\widetilde O(d)$ for sub-Gaussian data, (2) adapt its privacy noise to the intrinsic randomness of the data, and (3) extend seamlessly to any target dimension $k\le d$. However, its sample complexity has a suboptimal dependence on $k$. We propose the first algorithm that achieves optimal sample complexity in both $d$ and $k$, while retaining properties (2) and (3) of \kdppca. Additionally, prior utility guarantees require a minimum sample size with exponential dependence on the eigengap. Our method removes this dependence. It also improves the dependence on spectral parameters, matching known lower bounds for the spiked covariance model. Unlike deflation-based approaches like \kdppca, our algorithm updates the full $d\times k$ subspace jointly rather than one eigenvector at a time. This non-deflation structure simplifies the algorithm, reduces the number of hyper-parameters, and improves computational efficiency, particularly when using block linear algebra libraries.

Read more

entry.title: Orthogonal Updates for the Win: Towards Accelerated Adaptive Minimax Optimization

link.title: Orthogonal Updates for the Win: Towards Accelerated Adaptive Minimax Optimization

entry.content:
Single-loop minimax methods are appealing for modern machine learning, but standard stochastic gradient updates can be unstable and oscillatory under tightly coupled primal-dual dynamics, making performance notoriously sensitive to stepsizes. To fundamentally improve stability, we develop an orthogonal update framework tailored to minimax optimization, which applies updates along orthogonalized directions to reduce update anisotropy. However, orthogonalization reshapes the optimization geometry and makes coordinating primal-dual stepsizes even more delicate. To overcome this challenge, we develop AdaSGDA, which equips orthogonal updates with an adaptive stepsize rule driven by accumulated gradient norms. This mechanism automatically balances coupled primal-dual progress under orthogonalization, yielding an effectively parameter-free method for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization. We prove that AdaSGDA avoids problem-dependent tuning while attaining the state-of-the-art $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/4}\right)$ convergence rate. We further propose AdaSGDA-VR, which incorporates a carefully designed variance reduction scheme and achieves the faster $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/3}\right)$ rate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods deliver competitive performance compared to existing minimax optimization methods.

Read more

entry.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery

link.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery

entry.content:
Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

Read more

entry.title: Overlap-Excluded Estimation of Participation Probabilities for Non-Probability Samples

link.title: Overlap-Excluded Estimation of Participation Probabilities for Non-Probability Samples

entry.content:
Correction of selection bias is crucial for making valid statistical inferences about a finite population using non-probability datasets. Various approaches have been proposed to correct this bias and obtain estimates of finite population quantities such as means and totals. The quasi-randomisation approaches, in particular, aim to estimate a `participation probability’ for units in the non-probability dataset. These probabilities are then applied in an inverse probability weighting scheme to produce population estimates. In this paper, we propose to estimate the participation probabilities for the non-probability sample by combining the non-probability sample with an available probability sample, while excluding the overlapping units in the probability sample. When the true overlap cannot be determined, we show how the Expectation-Maximization method can be used to simultaneously estimate the overlap and the participation probabilities. We compare the performance of our approach against several alternative methods theoretically and in an empirical context, and demonstrate the efficiency gains that are possible when the overlapping probability sample is excluded.

Read more

entry.title: Panel Local Projections with Missing Data

link.title: Panel Local Projections with Missing Data

entry.content:
A panel local projection can remain identified even when missing data leave no complete regression case. We recover the projection over specified dates by combining factor-based conditional means with idiosyncratic covariances from observed pairs. Under strong factors in the auxiliary panel, sufficient factor variation at observed dates and enough observations of the required pairs, a second-order expansion yields bias-corrected moments and a joint score for inference. The localized multiplier bootstrap provides pointwise confidence intervals and simultaneous bands under additional dependence restrictions. We revisit the investment response to geopolitical risk studied by Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) with a larger quarterly firm sample and extend the analysis to monthly projections of trailing-three-month investment intensity. In the monthly analysis, the six-month response difference between high- and low-exposure firms becomes more negative as firms with incomplete histories enter the sample.

Read more

entry.title: Partition Tree: Conditional Density Estimation over General Outcome Spaces

link.title: Partition Tree: Conditional Density Estimation over General Outcome Spaces

entry.content:
We propose Partition Tree, a tree-based framework for conditional density estimation over general outcome spaces that supports both continuous and categorical variables within a unified formulation. Our approach models conditional distributions as piecewise-constant densities on data-adaptive partitions and learns trees by greedily minimizing a surrogate for conditional log-loss. This yields a scalable alternative to existing probabilistic trees that does not make parametric assumptions about the target distribution. We further introduce Partition Forest, an ensemble extension obtained by averaging conditional densities. Empirically, we demonstrate improved probabilistic prediction over CART-style trees and competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art probabilistic tree methods and Random Forests.

entry.title: Pause and Reflect: Conformal Aggregation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

link.title: Pause and Reflect: Conformal Aggregation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

entry.content:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with self-consistency improves performance by aggregating multiple sampled reasoning paths. In this setting, correctness is no longer tied to a single reasoning trace but to the aggregation rule over a pool of candidate paths, making aggregation uncertainty the central challenge. This issue is critical where confidently incorrect answers are far more costly than abstentions. We introduce a conformal procedure for CoT reasoning that directly addresses aggregation uncertainty. Our approach replaces majority voting with weighted score aggregation over reasoning paths and calibrates an abstention rule using conformal risk control. This approach leads to finite-sample guarantees on the confident-error rate–the probability that the system answers and is wrong. We further identify score separability as the key condition under which abstention provably improves selective accuracy, and derive closed-form expressions that predict accuracy gains from calibration data alone. The method is fully inference-time, and requires no retraining. Across four benchmarks, four open-source models, and three score classes, realized confident-error rates are consistent with the prescribed targets up to calibration-split and test-set variability. Our method achieves $90.1\%$ selective accuracy on GSM8K by abstaining on fewer than $5\%$ of problems, compared with $82.3\%$ accuracy under majority voting and $87.4\%$ under score-weighted voting without abstention, while conformal risk control keeps the expected rate of confidently wrong answers below $10\%$.

Read more

entry.title: Persistent-Transient Policy Evaluation for Markov Chains via Minimal Peripheral Quotients

link.title: Persistent-Transient Policy Evaluation for Markov Chains via Minimal Peripheral Quotients

entry.content:
We study fixed-policy evaluation for finite Markov chains that may be reducible and periodic. Classical evaluation methods with gain and bias decomposition are not always diagnostic: the gain records only invariant Ces`aro averages, while persistent phase-dependent behavior is absorbed into the bias together with genuinely transient effects. We identify the real peripheral invariant subspace $\mathcal{K}(P)$ of the transition matrix $P$ as the source of this ambiguity. Quotienting by $\mathcal{K}(P)$ is the minimal exact quotient that removes all non-decaying modes and makes the remaining dynamics strictly stable. After choosing a gauge projection $\Pi$ with kernel $\mathcal{K}(P)$, the reward admits a unique decomposition $r = g_\Pi^\star + (I-P)v_\Pi^\star$, where $g_\Pi^\star$ is a persistent regime profile and $v_\Pi^\star$ is a gauge-fixed transient component. An exact comparison with classical normalized gain and bias shows that the new pair reallocates the same information into a persistent profile and a gauge-fixed representative of the transient quotient. This decomposition reconstructs finite-horizon returns, recovers statewise average reward, admits a transient-cost interpretation, and yields a stable estimator under a generative model.

Read more

entry.title: Personalized Pricing with Invalid Instrumental Variables: Identification, Estimation, and Policy Learning

link.title: Personalized Pricing with Invalid Instrumental Variables: Identification, Estimation, and Policy Learning

entry.content:
Pricing based on individual customer characteristics is widely used to maximize sellers’ revenues. We study how a firm can learn such a personalized pricing policy from historical transactions when unobserved factors affect both the prices it charged and the revenue it earned. Standard instrumental variable (IV) methods either focus on a discrete treatment space or require that the IV affect revenue only through price. This exclusion restriction is difficult to justify in pricing, where the most natural candidate IVs are price-setting levers that may also affect revenue directly. We propose PRINT (Personalized pRicing using Invalid iNsTrumental variables), a policy learning method for continuous prices that uses such candidate IVs. Relying on structural models of revenue and price, we show that the optimal pricing policy can be identified with invalid IV that shifts higher moments of historical prices, when the unobserved factors that drive customers’ price sensitivity are separated from those used by the historical pricing rule. Based on this identification, which leads to conditional moment restrictions with generalized residual functions, we construct an adversarial min-max estimator that accommodates flexible machine learning models and establish regret bounds for the learned pricing policy. Simulation studies and an application to a U.S. online auto lender illustrate the method’s performance. Our results give a principled way to learn personalized prices from observational data using imperfect price-setting levers, and clarify when doing so is justified.

Read more

entry.title: Pion: A Spectrum-Preserving Optimizer via Orthogonal Equivalence Transformation

link.title: Pion: A Spectrum-Preserving Optimizer via Orthogonal Equivalence Transformation

entry.content:
We introduce Pion, a spectrum-preserving optimizer for large language model (LLM) training based on orthogonal equivalence transformation. Unlike additive optimizers such as Adam and Muon, Pion updates each weight matrix through left and right orthogonal transformations, preserving its singular values throughout training. This yields an optimization mechanism that modulates the geometry of weight matrices while keeping their spectral norm fixed. We derive the Pion update rule, systematically examine its design choices, and analyze its convergence behavior along with several key properties. Empirical results show that Pion offers a stable and competitive alternative to standard optimizers for both LLM pretraining and finetuning.

Read more

entry.title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets

link.title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets

entry.content:
Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.

Read more

entry.title: Prescriptive Learning of Linear Policies with Feasibility Guarantees for Binary Decision-Making

link.title: Prescriptive Learning of Linear Policies with Feasibility Guarantees for Binary Decision-Making

entry.content:
Binary decision-making under uncertainty arises across a wide range of applications, including energy systems scheduling, transportation, and workforce planning. While machine learning has been increasingly applied to accelerate or replace mixed-integer solvers in such settings, existing approaches rely on predictive learning, training models to reproduce optimal decisions from labeled data, which lacks knowledge of counterfactual outcomes and provides no guarantees that the resulting decisions will be feasible. This limitation is further compounded under distributional shift, where policies trained on historical data may produce systematically infeasible decisions. We propose a prescriptive learning framework for binary decision-making that addresses both limitations. Rather than predicting optimal labels, the framework jointly optimizes over linear decision policies and feasible assignments across all training scenarios, allowing feasible alternatives and their operational performance to be considered directly during training. We further extend the framework to a distributionally robust chance-constrained formulation using a Wasserstein ambiguity set, which enforces feasibility with a prescribed probability under the worst-case distribution in the ambiguity set and enables a tunable trade-off between robustness and solution quality. We demonstrate the framework on two case studies, namely a unit commitment problem and a staff allocation problem. Out-of-sample experiments under test distributions that either match or differ from the training distribution show that the robust model is more conservative when the two distributions coincide, while under distributional shift it substantially reduces unmet demand and lowers total cost by up to 76.5% relative to classical predictive learning.

entry.title: Private Sparse Sketches for Linear Regression

link.title: Private Sparse Sketches for Linear Regression

entry.content:
Sketching compresses a large dataset into a smaller summary, allowing regression on the sketch to approximate the full-data objective. A sketch released under differential privacy can be reused with any non-private regression solver, any number of times, without further privacy loss. We study private sparse sketches for $\ell_2$ and $\ell_1$ regression. We first prove lower bounds on the noise required by common sparse sketches for both problems when the sketching matrix is public. Since regression on a sketch can be solved without revealing the sketching matrix, we construct sketches whose randomness is kept secret. Hiding how individual records enter the sketch provides an additional source of privacy, allowing less noise for the same privacy guarantee. We prove differential privacy guarantees for both constructions, and experiments on real datasets show improved utility over public-sketch baselines.

Read more

entry.title: PromptShift-CRC: What Drift-Aware Weighting Adds to Online Conformal Risk Control for Foundation Models

link.title: PromptShift-CRC: What Drift-Aware Weighting Adds to Online Conformal Risk Control for Foundation Models

entry.content:
A risk threshold calibrated on old prompts can stop being valid when prompts to a foundation model drift. We study PromptShift-CRC, a rule that weights past prompts by feature similarity, falls back to recent prompts when the current prompt is unlike the past, and updates its level online. We prove that the update controls the long-run violation rate for any weights, so marginal coverage cannot separate weighting schemes. We give a conditional bound at a fixed level whose cost is a weighted total variation distance, bounded by a computable prompt-drift term up to an unknown Lipschitz constant. We propose a comparison protocol: a matched short-window baseline, a validity and sharpness frontier, 30-seed synthetic streams, and real-output streams ordered without using the model’s output. On MMLU, TruthfulQA (Qwen2.5-1.5B) and RealToxicityPrompts (GPT-2, replicated with a second generator and classifier), every online method reaches the target. PromptShift-CRC stays within 0.0055 of the Adaptive CRC frontier and avoids the worst window, but DtACI matches or beats it in most settings. The rule performs like a mid-ranked window without having to choose one. Tests fixed in advance to favor the weights show no consistent gain over the frontier. Code, outputs and streams are released.

Read more

entry.title: Proximal Difference-in-Differences for Causal Learning under Confounding and Outcome Drift

link.title: Proximal Difference-in-Differences for Causal Learning under Confounding and Outcome Drift

entry.content:
Estimating long-term treatment effects is essential in regulatory and healthcare decision-making, yet the limited follow-up duration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) poses a significant challenge. Open-label extension studies attempt to capture additional information for treated subjects, but there is often significant systematic censoring and selection bias due to placebo crossover. While supplementing RCTs with real-world evidence is a common strategy, existing methods often rely on restrictive exchangeability assumptions that fail under latent confounding. We propose a novel proximal framework to integrate real-world evidence into an RCT with an open-label extension to estimate the long-term continued-control trajectory. Our approach successfully identifies long-term effects even in the presence of time-varying latent confounding effects and inter-study outcome drift. We provide a doubly robust locally efficient estimator that provides further resilience to model misspecification. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework maintains validity in complex data-generating processes where standard approaches may be biased.

entry.title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment

link.title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment

entry.content:
AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.

Read more

entry.title: Quantifying Long-Range Dependence in Object-Valued Time Series

link.title: Quantifying Long-Range Dependence in Object-Valued Time Series

entry.content:
Object-valued time series, including distributions, covariance matrices, networks, and compositions, lack the linear structure required by conventional autocovariance-based definitions of long memory. We develop an intrinsic framework for defining and estimating long memory in metric spaces of negative type. An isometric embedding yields a centered Hilbert-valued process, and the trace of its lag-covariance operator provides a signed, additive measure of temporal dependence. Crucially, this trace equals the difference between the marginal mean pairwise distance and expected lagged distance, so the framework and its estimators use only distances between the original objects. We define the memory parameter through the nonsummable decay of this trace and show that it coincides with the usual parameter in Hilbert-valued settings. Estimation uses Bartlett aggregates of distance-based lag measures. Estimating the common marginal distance from the same dependent sample induces a common-centering bias in these aggregates. We derive its finite-sample form and propose iterated block-difference corrections, log-ratio and multi-bandwidth log-slope estimators, and a localized self-consistency refinement. We establish consistency, document substantial bias reduction in simulations, and find long-memory evidence in foreign-exchange return distributions and U.S. electricity-generation compositions.

Read more

entry.title: Query- and Candidate-Aware Long User Sequence Modeling for Sponsored Product Ranking in Search

link.title: Query- and Candidate-Aware Long User Sequence Modeling for Sponsored Product Ranking in Search

entry.content:
User sequence modeling is widely used in recommendation and advertising. Search ranking presents an additional challenge: the current query expresses immediate intent, while a candidate product determines which parts of a user’s long-term history are relevant. We present a production sequence framework for sponsored-product ranking that augments recent behavior with two retrieval channels over long-term history: candidate-nearest-neighbor retrieval and query-nearest-neighbor retrieval. The selected actions are encoded together with dedicated query and candidate context tokens, while candidate-aware early fusion injects the candidate into every history token. Offline ablations show that dual retrieval improves major ranking metrics relative to the production baseline. In an online A/B test on sponsored-product search traffic, the model increased CTR, attributed conversion rate, and orders per impression.

Read more
