entry.title: Rank-Transformed Dissimilarity Profiles for High-Dimensional Classification

link.title: Rank-Transformed Dissimilarity Profiles for High-Dimensional Classification

entry.content:
Despite advances in representation learning, high-dimensional classification remains challenging in low-sample-size regimes, where the dominant signal may vary across applications and labeled data are often limited. We propose a dissimilarity-profiling classification framework that represents each observation by its class-wise dissimilarity profile, transforming the original feature space into a low-dimensional representation that summarizes how the observation relates to each class. The key idea is to turn an effect of the curse of dimensionality into signal: high-dimensional geometry can induce systematic within-class and between-class dissimilarity patterns under location, scale, or other distributional changes, and these patterns are captured by the class-wise profiles. Building on this representation, we introduce a rank-transformed algorithm that converts dissimilarities into class-wise rank profiles. The proposed method delivers competitive or improved performance relative to commonly used classifiers on two-class, multi-class, network, and real high-dimensional low-sample-size datasets. To clarify the underlying mechanism, we characterize the mean and covariance of a distance-based surrogate, showing how location, scale, and higher-order distributional features enter the profile representation. Contamination experiments show that the rank transformation can improve robustness. The same profile construction applies to non-Euclidean data whenever pairwise dissimilarities can be computed.

Read more

entry.title: Regularity in Cryptocurrency Market Cycles: A Halving-to-Halving Analysis Using Data from Google Trends and Wikipedia

link.title: Regularity in Cryptocurrency Market Cycles: A Halving-to-Halving Analysis Using Data from Google Trends and Wikipedia

entry.content:
Bitcoin halvings provide a natural temporal structure for studying long-term dynamics of cryptocurrency markets. This paper presents a methodological framework for analyzing the regularity of Bitcoin and aggregate cryptocurrency market cycles by normalizing historical periods between consecutive halving events and projecting them onto a common relative-time scale expressed as the percentage of cycle completion. The proposed framework integrates market variables, namely Bitcoin price and aggregate cryptocurrency market capitalization, with measures of public attention derived from Google Trends search volume and Wikipedia pageviews. To obtain long-horizon daily attention indices, Google Trends data are reconstructed from overlapping 90-day windows linked by median scale ratios, following established approaches to combining high-frequency Google Trends samples. Rather than attempting to forecast future prices, the study aims to compare historical cycles, identify recurring temporal patterns, and evaluate the relationship between market dynamics and retail investor interest across different cycle-relative stages. Exploratory results point to a possible recurring structure. The maxima of the aggregate market capitalization in the two most recent completed cycles occurred at 39.0% and 37.9% of cycle completion, and the highest value of the ongoing cycle observed to date at 38.1% (534-547 days after the respective halvings), although the corresponding multiple of the halving-day value fell from 66 to 1.8. Public attention shows a similar compression of peak multiples, but not a similar timing. The paper also discusses current data limitations and outlines future research directions, including formal lead-lag analyses and expanded multi-asset investigations.

Read more

entry.title: Reliable Chain-of-Thought via Prefix Consistency

link.title: Reliable Chain-of-Thought via Prefix Consistency

entry.content:
Large language models often improve accuracy on reasoning tasks by sampling multiple chain-of-thought (CoT) traces and aggregating them with majority voting, a test-time technique called self-consistency. When we truncate a CoT partway through and regenerate the remainder, we observe that traces with correct answers reproduce their original answer more often than traces with wrong answers. We use this difference as a reliability signal, prefix consistency, that weights each candidate answer by how often it reappears under regeneration. It requires no access to token log-probabilities or self-rating prompts. Across five reasoning models and four math and science benchmarks, prefix consistency is the best correctness predictor in most settings, and reweighting votes by this signal reaches the plateau accuracy of majority voting with up to $21\times$ fewer tokens (median $4.6\times$). Our code is available at https://github.com/naoto-iwase/prefix-consistency.

Read more

Across five reasoning models and four math and science benchmarks, prefix consistency is the best correctness predictor in most settings, and reweighting votes by this signal reaches the plateau accuracy of majority voting with up to $21\times$ fewer tokens (median $4.6\times$). Our code is available at https://github.com/naoto-iwase/prefix-consistency.

entry.title: Renewable model averaging for generalized linear models

link.title: Renewable model averaging for generalized linear models

entry.content:
Prediction is one of the most important research topics in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, in the domain of streaming data analysis, real-time prediction has become a rapidly growing research field in recent years, owing to the abundance of streaming data. In many fields of scientific research, such as biomedical research, weather forecasting, and traffic management, improving real-time prediction of streaming data is crucial in general. However, the complicated features of streaming data, such as large-scale and high-velocity, impose both theoretical and computational challenges to the development and evaluation of real-time prediction in this field, especially when the investigator has multiple models at hand. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel Renewable Model Averaging method through Quadratic approximation (ReMAQ) for generalized linear model (GLM) for streaming data. By approximating the model averaging procedure for GLMs (which is typically a convex optimization problem) with a quadratic optimization formulation, ReMAQ allows us to update the model averaging prediction sequentially when a new batch of data arrives, without accessing the entire historical data. Moreover, ReMAQ is also computationally efficient as one only needs to consider a quadratic programming problem in each steps of updating. Under certain regular conditions, we also show that the proposed ReMAQ weight is asymptotically equivalent to that by the oracle model averaging based on the inaccessible full data, the asymptotic optimality of ReMAQ is then established accordingly. The proposed method is also assessed by simulation studies. We apply our proposed ReMAQ in the study of the Airline On-Time Performance Dataset and the results demonstrate the superiority our method in practical situations.

Read more

entry.title: Reusable Conditional Resampling via Flow Matching for Constraint-Based Causal Discovery

link.title: Reusable Conditional Resampling via Flow Matching for Constraint-Based Causal Discovery

entry.content:
Constraint-based causal discovery requires many conditional independence (CI) tests. Generative CI tests are attractive in nonlinear and high-dimensional settings because they can model complex conditional distributions, but often suffer from high per-test costs and limited reusability across query-dependent conditional resampling tasks in graph search. We propose a generative nonlinear CI testing and graph search framework for PC-style causal discovery. We introduce Langevin-RePaint for conditional imputation. Building on Langevin-RePaint and joint flow matching modeling, we propose the Flow Matching based Conditional Independence Test (FMCIT), which reformulates generative CI testing from query-specific conditional modeling into a reusable conditional resampling framework. We establish theoretical guarantees for FMCIT’s type-I error control. FMCIT reuses a single trained generative model to generate randomized copies throughout graph search. We then introduce GPC-FMCIT, which embeds FMCIT into a guided PC pipeline with screening, guidance, refinement, and orientation. By using low-cost screening to shrink the search space, constructing edge-specific candidate conditioning sets from local graph structure, and invoking FMCIT only in a budget-controlled refinement stage, GPC-FMCIT reduces both the deployment cost of individual nonlinear CI queries and the overall query complexity. On synthetic nonlinear structural equation models, GPC-FMCIT improves CPDAG recovery over PC-stable baselines and requires far fewer FMCIT queries than direct FMCIT-based PC search, and on hESC gene-expression data it yields smaller graphs than PC/FisherZ in a descriptive comparison. Overall, our results suggest that, through the joint design of reusable conditional resampling and controlled graph search, generative nonlinear CI testing can become a practical component of PC-style causal discovery.

entry.title: Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares

link.title: Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares

entry.content:
Many scientific responses take values in Riemannian manifolds, with predictors that are scalar- and/or manifold-valued. A regression analysis in such settings must provide accurate prediction with hypothesis testing for individual coefficients. Yet no current manifold-regression framework accommodates both predictor types and enables per-coefficient hypothesis tests. We propose Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares (ROLS) as a tangent space conditional-mean model, which is the ordinary least squares (OLS) analogue for Riemannian manifolds. ROLS is well-defined under an explicit injectivity condition that keeps the logarithm maps single-valued, with cut-locus conditions for branch-sensitive cases outside it. Within the local geometric setting it admits a closed-form estimator, an $O(n^{-1})$ excess prediction-error bound with explicit curvature bias, and asymptotic $t$- and Wald tests for individual coefficients. With synthetic simulations and three real-data case studies, ROLS is shown to be competitive with the state-of-the-art baselines. In addition, the per-coefficient tests agree with effects reported in literature. We envision ROLS to be a standard tool for manifold-valued regression with coefficient-level inference to support scientific discovery, which can be interpreted in the same way as Euclidean OLS. The source code is available at https://github.com/XiaoyuChenPub/ROLS.

Read more

entry.title: Robust Gaussian process regression: posterior contraction

link.title: Robust Gaussian process regression: posterior contraction

entry.content:
Gaussian processes form a popular and flexible class of prior distributions with principled uncertainty quantification, but the Gaussian likelihood on which the corresponding posterior relies makes them highly sensitive to outliers and contaminated observations. We study Gaussian process regression when among the $n$ observations, $m$ of these are possibly contaminated. A generic framework to obtain posterior contraction rates in this setting is considered, from a frequentist perspective as the sample size $n$ and the number of corrupted observations $m$ grow. We adopt a generalized Bayes approach in which the log–likelihood is replaced by a robustified version; we discuss various choices thereof, such as one recently proposed by Altamirano et al. that preserves conjugacy. We investigate the minimax rate of estimation under adversarial contamination in terms of the Sobolev smoothness $\beta$ of the regression function and $m$. The question of building adaptive procedures to both $\beta$ and $m$ is investigated, and we show that a polynomial loss for adaptation must be paid in general. We instantiate our results for Mat'ern Gaussian process and deep ReLU network priors. Numerical experiments for existing and new robust algorithms are provided, illustrating the practical applicability of our results.

Read more

entry.title: Robust Machine Learning for Regulatory Sequence Modeling under Biological and Technical Distribution Shifts

link.title: Robust Machine Learning for Regulatory Sequence Modeling under Biological and Technical Distribution Shifts

entry.content:
Robust machine learning for regulatory genomics is studied under biologically and technically induced distribution shifts. Deep convolutional and attention-based models achieve strong in-distribution performance on DNA regulatory sequence prediction tasks but are usually evaluated under i.i.d. assumptions, even though real applications involve cell type-specific programs, evolutionary turnover, assay protocol changes, and sequencing artifacts. We introduce a robustness framework that combines a mechanistic simulation benchmark with real data analysis on an MPRA dataset to quantify performance degradation, calibration failures, and uncertainty-based reliability. In simulation, motif-driven regulatory outputs are generated with cell type-specific programs, PWM perturbations, GC bias, depth variation, batch effects, and heteroscedastic noise, and CNN, BiLSTM, and transformer models are evaluated. Models remain accurate and reasonably calibrated under mild GC content shifts but show higher error, severe variance miscalibration, and coverage collapse under motif effect rewiring and noise-dominated regimes, revealing robustness gaps invisible to standard i.i.d. evaluation. Adding simple biological structural priors, motif-derived features in simulation, and global GC content in MPRA improves distribution error and yields consistent robustness gains under biologically meaningful genomic shifts, while providing only limited protection against strong assay noise. Uncertainty-aware selective prediction offers an additional safety layer, and risk coverage analyses on simulated and MPRA data show that filtering low-confidence inputs recovers low-risk subsets, including under GC-based OOD conditions, although reliability gains diminish when noise dominates.

Read more

entry.title: Robust Posterior Projection for Bayesian Inference Under Order Restrictions

link.title: Robust Posterior Projection for Bayesian Inference Under Order Restrictions

entry.content:
In archaeology and geochronology, stratigraphic information constrains the relative chronological order of dated samples. Bayesian chronological models incorporate these constraints either through the prior, or by projecting an unconstrained posterior distribution onto the set of ordered chronologies. Dating measurements may nevertheless appear inconsistent with their stratigraphic position, owing to disturbances that do not justify discarding them. We introduce different robust projection maps based on the Huber loss and characterize the non-uniqueness of the considered maps which justifies a Tikhonov regularization. The robust maps also decompose each sample into a monotone baseline and a spike, which flags questionable samples. We adapt the Sequential Block Merging algorithm for the Huber-type losses, and propose a data-driven heuristic for selecting the hyperparameter on which each loss depends on. Simulation studies and geochronological case studies illustrate the gains in robustness and their limits.

Read more

entry.title: Robust Satisficing Ensemble: Scalable Model Aggregation Under Distribution Shifts

link.title: Robust Satisficing Ensemble: Scalable Model Aggregation Under Distribution Shifts

entry.content:
Standard ensemble methods can improve robustness by mitigating individual model stochasticity, but they frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution, leaving systems vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We introduce the Robust Satisficing Ensemble (RSE), a scalable probabilistic aggregation framework designed to secure model combinations by minimizing their fragility against distributional changes. By bridging a robust satisficing objective with a quadratic risk surrogate, RSE derives an analytical inner adversary. This fundamental reformulation enables highly efficient weight updates without the computational bottleneck of standard minimax optimization, crucially decoupling optimization complexity from sample size to scale effectively to large datasets. In particular, we prove a geometrically decaying truncation error for the fragility approximation via Lagrange-Burmann expansion and establish stationarity guarantees for RSE. We evaluate RSE across a comprehensive spectrum of distribution shifts, including adversarial label shift (SST-5, TREC), natural subpopulation and temporal shifts (CivilComments, HuffPost). Our results demonstrate that RSE consistently outperforms strong robust baselines, including GroupDRO, IRM, and SRM. These findings establish RSE as a practical, theoretically grounded safeguard for reliable model aggregation in dynamic environments.

Read more

entry.title: SAMBoost: Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting

link.title: SAMBoost: Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting

entry.content:
We propose SAMBoost (Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting), a gradient boosting method that combines tree-based covariate modelling with a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) latent spatial field through a single penalised objective. At each boosting iteration, the predictor is decomposed into separate covariate and spatial components. The method is motivated by applications in which the spatial effect is not a nuisance to be removed but a quantity of interest that must be recovered alongside the covariates. In insurance, for example, practitioners need both flexible nonlinear covariate effects and an interpretable geographic risk surface that can be reported on its own. Existing approaches often involve trade-offs, offering flexible covariate modelling but no explicit spatial field, rigorous spatial inference with a fixed additive covariate structure, or a combination of both at computational costs that limit practicality for large datasets. SAMBoost addresses these goals within the boosting loop, and the underlying mesh produces a sparse precision structure whose cost is largely independent of sample size. On simulations and on an open benchmark, SAMBoost matches or improves on the predictive accuracy of joint Gaussian process and tree boosting approaches. It is also faster and recovers the spatial field and covariate effects more accurately. When covariate effects include interactions, it outperforms additive Bayesian spatial models. Applied to a flood insurance portfolio with 4.9 million records, SAMBoost trains on the full training set without subsampling and runs about sixteen times faster than a Bayesian reference, with a consistent spatial risk surface. A public Python implementation is available.

Read more

entry.title: SGD in Multiclass Logistic Regression: Sequential Learning and Scaling Laws

link.title: SGD in Multiclass Logistic Regression: Sequential Learning and Scaling Laws

entry.content:
We study the training dynamics of multiclass logistic regression on high-dimensional mixture models with a large number of classes and establish precise scaling laws governing the cross-entropy risk under gradient-based optimization. We show that learning proceeds sequentially across classes, from most to least frequent. When the class priors follow a power law distribution, the risk dynamics decompose into three phases: an initial plateau until the first class is learned, a power-law decay regime during which sequential learning occurs, and a final convergence regime. We then analyze how model capacity interacts with optimization under a fixed compute budget. When the effective dimension is restricted via projection onto leading principal components, the risk decomposes into a capacity term (a power law in the retained dimension) and an optimization term (a power law in training time). Optimizing this tradeoff yields a compute-optimal scaling law for logistic regression, with explicit prescriptions for model size and training time as functions of compute. These results extend theoretical scaling laws from linear regression to multiclass classification, while connecting to empirical scaling laws observed in large-scale neural networks.

entry.title: Sampling-Free Privacy Accounting for Matrix Mechanisms under Random Allocation

link.title: Sampling-Free Privacy Accounting for Matrix Mechanisms under Random Allocation

entry.content:
We study privacy amplification for differentially private model training with matrix factorization under random allocation (also known as the balls-in-bins model). Recent work by Choquette-Choo et al. (2025) proposes a sampling-based Monte Carlo approach to compute amplification parameters in this setting. However, their guarantees either only hold with some high probability or require random abstention by the mechanism. Furthermore, the required number of samples for ensuring $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP is inversely proportional to $\delta$. In contrast, we develop sampling-free bounds based on R'enyi divergence and conditional composition. The former is facilitated by a dynamic programming formulation to efficiently compute the bounds. The latter complements it by offering stronger privacy guarantees for small $\epsilon$, where R'enyi divergence bounds inherently lead to an over-approximation. Our framework applies to arbitrary banded and non-banded matrices. Through numerical comparisons, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach across a broad range of matrix mechanisms used in research and practice.

Read more

entry.title: Scale-Invariant Empirical-Bayes Laplace Approximation for ReLU Networks

link.title: Scale-Invariant Empirical-Bayes Laplace Approximation for ReLU Networks

entry.content:
ReLU networks are well-known to have continuous scale symmetries; infinitely many reparameterized weight vectors that represent the same function. Dinh et al. (2017) have shown that, by reparameterizing, the geometry of the loss landscape (e.g., curvature) of these networks can be changed arbitrarily without affecting the underlying function. Thus, any quantity that depends on the network’s geometry should be defined with care. In this paper, we show that the Empirical Bayes (EB) Laplace’s approximation is not well-defined for ReLU networks, mainly due to Hessian dependence in computing the marginal likelihood, which is not invariant under ReLU scale symmetries. Thus, we can get different prior precisions, posterior covariances, and predictive uncertainties for a network having identical predictions under ReLU scaling. We define family of prior precision fields indexed by $\gamma$ and introduce $\gamma$-canonicalization, which first converts the network to its canonical representation by balancing the ratio of incoming to outgoing weights, and then fits the Empirical Bayes (EB) Laplace to the canonical representation. This procedure is equivalent to transporting the isotropic Gaussian prior from the canonical representation to the original coordinates, by producing a ReLU-scale-compatible precision field. This makes the marginal likelihood invariant under ReLU scaling, while allowing $\gamma$ to be selected by maximizing the marginal likelihood. The resulting EB Laplace approximation is well-defined on ReLU scale-equivalence classes and yields consistent prior precision selection and predictive uncertainties across functionally identical parameterizations.

Read more

entry.title: Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis

link.title: Schrödinger–Föllmer Actor–Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis

entry.content:
Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions, but a $Q$-weighted update does not specify how to sample from the resulting target distribution. We propose Schr"odinger–F"ollmer Actor–Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) method for Kullback–Leibler (KL)-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. A minimax Bellman critic estimates the action-value function, which defines an exponentially tilted target policy. A Doob $h$-transform expresses this update as a correction to the reference diffusion drift. The target drift is a weighted conditional mean of Brownian-bridge labels. We fit it by weighted regression using endpoints from the current policy and pointwise action-value evaluations. In the small-update regime, the KL-regularized update follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds that separate the errors from critic estimation, weighted neural drift regression, and diffusion discretization through a reverse-KL actor bound. The average-performance bound depends explicitly on the comparison coefficients over the policy iterations. Across six D4RL offline-to-online tasks, the final scores of the $Q$-guided bridge-regression implementation exceed its offline initialization on every task and Cal-QL on five tasks. We also compare with offline RL and online-only baselines.

Read more

entry.title: Selected-Risk Calibration for Feasibility at Returned Decisions

link.title: Selected-Risk Calibration for Feasibility at Returned Decisions

entry.content:
When an optimization problem uses a surrogate constraint, a decision that is feasible for the surrogate need not be feasible for the true constraint. We propose Selected-Risk Calibration (SRC), a framework that calibrates a learned constraint against the optimizer’s returned decisions for objectives drawn from a given distribution. SRC guarantees that, with probability at least $1-\delta$, every margin it certifies on held-out objectives has selected risk, the probability that the returned decision is infeasible, of at most $\gamma$. We also show that the random-input coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction does not bound the selected risk, and that likelihood-ratio reweighting for feedback covariate shift does not apply when the learned constraint is active at the returned decision. Our experiments show that a conformal margin covering about $90\%$ of random inputs covered as few as $17\%$ of the returned decisions, and every certified margin had a violation rate below its target on unseen objectives. Moreover, at equal cost, SRC’s correction had fewer or equal infeasible solutions to the baselines in 57 of 62 comparisons. The SRC framework applies to any setting in which a surrogate model chooses a decision whose feasibility can be verified for a sample of instances.

Read more

entry.title: Semiparametric causal mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials with post-treatment confounding

link.title: Semiparametric causal mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials with post-treatment confounding

entry.content:
Causal mediation analysis of cluster-randomized trials can reveal how interventions affect outcomes through individual and spillover pathways. Most existing methods target natural mediation effects under assumptions that exclude treatment-induced mediator–outcome confounding. We develop a semiparametric framework for interventional mediation effects that accommodates such confounding and within-cluster interference without requiring cross-world independence assumptions. We identify cluster-average and individual-average direct and indirect effects and decompose the indirect effect into individual and spillover components, distinguishing pathways through an individual’s own mediator and those of other cluster members. These contrasts evaluate hypothetical interventions on the joint mediator distribution and can differ from treatment effects carried through individual causal pathways represented by natural effects, thereby providing an intervention-oriented perspective that complements natural effects. We derive efficient influence functions to construct estimators using cluster-level cross-fitting, characterize their multiple-robustness properties, and establish conditions for asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency. To facilitate implementation, we develop a lower-dimensional reparameterization that reduces the need for multivariate density estimation and integration and allows nuisance functions to be estimated using parametric models or machine learning. Simulation studies evaluate finite-sample performance, and an application to a cluster-randomized trial of cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain illustrates the proposed methods.

Read more

entry.title: Separate versus Pooled Winsorization in Difference-in-Differences: Bias, Efficiency, and Finite-Sample Guarantees

link.title: Separate versus Pooled Winsorization in Difference-in-Differences: Bias, Efficiency, and Finite-Sample Guarantees

entry.content:
\textit{\textbf{Problem Definition: }} Extreme outcomes are common in operational data, and empirical difference-in-differences (DiD) studies often winsorize them to limit their influence. Yet winsorization can change both the estimated treatment effect and its sampling uncertainty. We ask when winsorization improves DiD estimation and whether cutoffs should be computed separately within each group-period cell or from observations pooled across cells. \textit{\textbf{Methodology/Results: }} We develop finite-sample and asymptotic analyses in a two-group, two-period DiD setting. For continuous outcomes with finite variance, separate winsorization achieves a uniform sub-Gaussian deviation guarantee under a calibrated winsorization fraction, while neither raw DiD nor pooled winsorization can achieve the same guarantee. We identify conditions under which separate winsorization is asymptotically unbiased, whereas pooled winsorization with a fixed fraction may remain biased. Under these conditions, standard tail classifications alone do not establish an efficiency ranking. Yet a two-sided decreasing-failure-rate (DFR) condition on each cell’s error distribution can guarantee strictly smaller asymptotic variance for separate winsorization than for raw DiD at every fixed winsorization fraction. Numerical results support both analyses. \textit{\textbf{Managerial Implications: }} Our results guide practitioners on whether and how to winsorize outcomes in DiD studies, clarifying the advantages and limitations of raw DiD, separate winsorization, and pooled winsorization. The DFR condition arising from our efficiency analysis offers a simple diagnostic for when winsorization can be expected to lower asymptotic variance while keeping the treatment-effect estimate unbiased, giving theoretical grounding to a practice that has so far rested mainly on convention.

Read more

entry.title: Separation Is a Riesz Energy: How Many Environments Does ICA Need?

link.title: Separation Is a Riesz Energy: How Many Environments Does ICA Need?

entry.content:
How many environments and samples does it take to separate $d$ Gaussian sources whose variances change across environments? Each source has a signature, its vector of variances. The Riesz $2$-energy $E_j$ of source $j$ sums the inverse Fisher informations for rotating it towards other sources. With known whitening, we prove a worst-case squared-angle risk lower bound of order $E_j/(n+E_j)$ for orthogonal estimators at every $n$ and $d$. A quadratic pencil given the signatures attains $E_j/n$ up to a constant above a separation-dependent sample threshold, even with estimated whitening. For well-spread signatures at fixed $K$, the energy grows as $d^2$, $d\log d$ and $d$ for $K=2$, $3$ and $K\ge4$, respectively. A design with $K\asymp\log d$ and pairwise Fisher information bounded below by a constant makes $d\log d$ samples sufficient. The eigenvectors of a single fixed linear combination have an average first-order error coefficient of at least order $d^2$. Simulations up to $d=1000$ support the first-order predictions, and on task fMRI the energy helps rank split-half instability.

Read more

entry.title: Sequential anomaly identification with sampling constraints for composite hypotheses

link.title: Sequential anomaly identification with sampling constraints for composite hypotheses

entry.content:
We consider the problem of sequential anomaly identification with sampling constraints, where multiple independent data sources are observed over time, but only a limited subset can be sampled at each instant. The objective is to identify the anomalous sources while controlling the probabilities of at least one false alarm and at least one missed detection below prescribed levels. An identification policy must jointly determine when to stop sampling, which sources to declare anomalous, and how to allocate observations across sources under the sampling constraints. We seek policies that minimize the expected time to decision to a first-order asymptotic approximation as the error probabilities vanish. The observations from each source follow an unknown density belonging to one of two disjoint sets, corresponding to regular and anomalous behavior. Focusing on a nonparametric framework, which allows greater flexibility in modeling regular and anomalous statistical behavior, we establish general conditions for asymptotic optimality and provide a unified characterization of asymptotically optimal policies for composite hypothesis testing under sampling constraints. Simulation results illustrate the performance of the proposed policies, and the robustness of the nonparametric framework.

Read more

entry.title: Severity-Controlled Prediction Sets for Medication Recommendation

link.title: Severity-Controlled Prediction Sets for Medication Recommendation

entry.content:
Medication recommendation is a multi-label prediction task. However, existing prediction-set evaluation and calibration methods rely mainly on exact-overlap metrics and therefore treat all missed medications as equally severe, overlooking how closely the prediction set matches them within the medication hierarchy. To address this, we introduce Conformal Severity Control (CSC), a post-hoc framework for calibrating medication prediction sets under hierarchy-aware mismatch severity. CSC uses the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) hierarchy to quantify mismatch severity and controls patient-level severity without retraining the predictor, supporting both average severity and upper-quantile severity for the highest-severity mismatches. Experiments on MIMIC-IV show that CSC tracks user-specified severity tolerances and shifts prediction sets away from distant mismatches toward exact or close matches.

Read more

entry.title: Sharp Regret Bounds and a Task-Covariance Correction for Spectral Representation Learning

link.title: Sharp Regret Bounds and a Task-Covariance Correction for Spectral Representation Learning

entry.content:
Spectral contrastive learning keeps the $k$ directions along which two views of the data depend most strongly, while downstream tasks may need other directions. Existing guarantees for spectral features assume that the distribution of tasks has no preferred direction. We show that this isotropy condition is the wrong criterion. With linear probing, the task distribution affects the average probing gain only through the matrix $B\Lambda B^\top$, where $B$ records the dependence between views and $\Lambda$ is the task covariance: optimal features span its top-$k$ eigenspace, whereas spectral features span that of $BB^\top$. Transfer therefore depends on alignment, and strongly uneven task preferences cost nothing when they favour the spectral directions. Otherwise the regret of spectral features is at most linear in the anisotropy of $\Lambda$. No representation chosen without task information improves this rate when the leading spectrum is flat, and a spectral gap makes it quadratic. With labelled tasks, the same matrix gives a correction: Fisher discriminant directions for a frozen encoder, or a one-term change to the spectral contrastive loss. We bound the regret of the correction by the error in estimating $B\Lambda B^\top$, and compare this error with the misalignment of spectral features to decide when to correct. The analysis extends to finite samples, continuous variables and noisy views. Correction reduces synthetic held-out regret from $0.858$ to $0.003$ with $2000$ labelled tasks, and the decision rule gives the lowest regret among the tested rules at every bank size. On CIFAR-100, spectral features of frozen encoders keep most of the task signal on unseen classes, and where a bank of other classes would lower accuracy, the rule keeps them in every case.

Read more

entry.title: Sharp bounds for posterior causal attribution given complete factual records

link.title: Sharp bounds for posterior causal attribution given complete factual records

entry.content:
Retrospective causal attribution evaluates whether altering an earlier event would have prevented an observed outcome. Observational data determine marginal potential-response probabilities at fixed inputs while leaving cross-world joint distributions unspecified. Conditional on a complete factual record in a finite Markovian structural causal model, independence across mechanisms is preserved and each unobserved conditional response distribution is restricted to a capped probability simplex. Every collection of conditional distributions satisfying these local bounds is jointly attainable within a single compatible structural causal model. Optimizing the counterfactual expectation over the resulting product domain yields sharp attribution bounds for multistage interventions and mediated effects, and compatible response-vector polytopes extend these bounds to structural response restrictions. Exact algorithms for causal chains and general directed acyclic graphs, consistent plug-in endpoint estimators, and finite-sample and asymptotic confidence intervals are developed and illustrated using synthetic reactor experiments and health survey data.

Read more

entry.title: Short-term associations between wild-bird and mammalian high pathogenic avian influenza detection in the United States

link.title: Short-term associations between wild-bird and mammalian high pathogenic avian influenza detection in the United States

entry.content:
High pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) detections in mammals have raised concern about repeated wildlife spillover and the targeting of mammalian surveillance. We evaluated whether wild-bird detection records contained short-term explanatory and predictive information about mammalian detections in the United States. Public surveillance records from April 2022 to July 2026 comprised 18,523 wild-bird and 815 mammalian detections. Monthly state-level mammalian counts were analysed using negative-binomial mixed models adjusted for seasonality, preceding mammalian detections and state-level heterogeneity. The selected model contained contemporaneous and one-month-lagged same-state wild-bird counts. A doubling of one plus the contemporaneous wild-bird count was associated with a 57.9% increase in the expected mammalian count (95% CI 43.5-73.8%), and a doubling of the preceding-month count with a 15.9% increase (5.2-27.8%). Bordering-state exposure did not improve fit. In a six-month temporal holdout, adding same-state wild-bird exposure reduced mean absolute error by 23.8% and root mean squared error by 27.9%, although total detections remained overpredicted. After exact-row deduplication, the corresponding effects were 59.7% and 13.3%. Wild-bird surveillance records contained short-term, geographically local information about mammalian HPAI detection activity, but the associations do not establish direct transmission and require further calibration before operational forecasting.

Read more

entry.title: Signed-Permutation Coordinate Transport for RMSNorm Transformers

link.title: Signed-Permutation Coordinate Transport for RMSNorm Transformers

entry.content:
Modern LLM workflows move coordinate-indexed objects across checkpoints: steering vectors, sparse autoencoders, top-$k$ neuron sets, attribution lists, LoRA updates, optimizer states, and merge alignments. This requires fixing the model’s residual-stream gauge. We show that the native coordinate-preserving orthogonal gauge is architecture-dependent: LayerNorm residual charts have permutation gauge $S_d$ up to a global sign flip, while RMSNorm charts with generic gains have signed-permutation gauge $B_d = S_d \ltimes {\pm 1}^d$. Permutation-only alignment is thus symmetry-incomplete for RMSNorm models. We introduce sign-marginalized Hungarian matching and prove that with decorrelated coordinates, signed-correlation matching has a permutation-accuracy ceiling equal to the true gauge’s positive-sign fraction up to $O(d 2^{-d})$, which sign-marginalized matching removes. Omitting signs induces expected squared error $2|\Delta W|_F^2$ on weight updates and loses orientation on vectors and AdamW first moments, while RMSNorm gains and AdamW second moments permute without signs. Controlled tests confirm these laws: a Qwen2.5-1.5B SST-2 LoRA adapter retains 0.944 accuracy (from 0.945) under $B_d$ transport vs. 0.523 under $S_d$, and steering preserves effects to $<10^{-4}$ at zero raw top-10 overlap. Across natural checkpoints, inherited slots suffice for same-base descendants (96.2%-100% retention), whereas cross-generation pairs support sparse prompt-stable subsets with causally decisive negative signs ($+0.185$ vs. $-0.010$ at $8\sigma$ on Qwen2/2.5-0.5B; $+0.189$ vs. $-0.021$ on 1.5B). Along fine-tuning trajectories, composing local $B_d$ gauges recovers 91.1% of cross-run Qwen2.5-1.5B coordinates at 1,500 steps vs. 60.3% for endpoint matching. Merge and interpretability audits confirm that coordinate names are reproducible only relative to an explicit $B_d$ gauge.

Read more

entry.title: Simulation Studies For Goodness-of-Fit and Two-Sample Methods For Univariate Data

link.title: Simulation Studies For Goodness-of-Fit and Two-Sample Methods For Univariate Data

entry.content:
We present the results of a large number of simulation studies regarding the power of various goodness-of-fit as well as nonparametric two-sample tests for univariate data. This includes both continuous and discrete data. In general no single method can be relied upon to provide good power, any one method may be quite good for some combination of null hypothesis and alternative and may fail badly for another. Based on the results of these studies we propose a fairly small number of methods chosen such that for any of the case studies included here at least one of the methods has good power. The studies were carried out using the R packages R2sample and Rgof, available from CRAN.

Read more

entry.title: Singular Bayesian Neural Networks

link.title: Singular Bayesian Neural Networks

entry.content:
Bayesian neural networks promise calibrated uncertainty but require $O(mn)$ parameters for standard mean-field Gaussian posteriors. We argue this cost is often unnecessary, particularly when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay. By parameterizing weights as $W = AB^{\top}$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$, we induce a posterior that is \emph{singular} with respect to the Lebesgue measure, concentrating on the rank-$r$ manifold. This singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field’s independence assumption. We derive PAC-Bayes generalization bounds whose complexity term scales as $\sqrt{r(m+n)}$ instead of $\sqrt{m n}$, and prove loss bounds that decompose the error into optimization and rank-induced bias using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem. We further adapt recent Gaussian complexity bounds for low-rank deterministic networks to Bayesian predictive means. Empirically, across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers on standard benchmarks, our method achieves competitive predictive performance while using up to $33\times$ fewer parameters than 5-member Deep Ensembles. It substantially improves OOD detection and often improves calibration relative to mean-field and perturbation baselines, while Deep Ensembles can still be stronger on in-distribution likelihood-based metrics.

Read more

entry.title: Smoothed Score Queries and the Complexity of Sampling

link.title: Smoothed Score Queries and the Complexity of Sampling

entry.content:
We study the query complexity of sampling from high-dimensional Gaussian distributions using gradient information. In the standard oracle model, exact gradients expose only matrix-vector products with the precision matrix, leading to polynomial approximation barriers and a characteristic $\sqrt{\kappa}$ dependence on the known spectral range. We show that this barrier disappears when the sampler is allowed to query smoothed scores, namely gradients of the logarithms of the Gaussian-convolved densities. For a centered Gaussian target with precision matrix $\Lambda$, a smoothed-score query at noise level $\tau$ gives access to the resolvent $(\Lambda+\tau^{-1}I)^{-1}$. Combining geometrically spaced noise levels with sinc-quadrature rational approximation, we obtain a sampler with $q=O((\log\kappa+\log(e\sqrt d/\delta_{\rm TV}))\log(e\sqrt d/\delta_{\rm TV}))$ smoothed-score queries for total variation error $\delta_{\rm TV}$, improving the condition-number dependence from $\sqrt{\kappa}$ to logarithmic. We also study finite-bit gradient oracles. Using coordinatewise quantization of the transformed smoothed-score answers and a final dithering step, we obtain a sampling scheme whose total communicated gradient information is polylogarithmic in $\kappa$; in particular, for fixed dimension and accuracy, the bit complexity is $O(\log^2\kappa)$. To complement these upper bounds, we introduce a channel-synthesis, or reverse-Shannon, converse technique for sampling lower bounds. This converts total-variation simulation guarantees into communication requirements and yields an $\Omega(d\log\kappa)$ bit lower bound for $d\ge2$ and fixed total variation error below one, as $\kappa\to\infty$. Together, these results identify smoothed scores as a provably more informative oracle for sampling and give nearly matching upper and lower bounds for its finite-bit complexity.

author.name: Jingbo Liu

entry.summary: We study the query complexity of sampling from high-dimensional Gaussian distributions using gradient information. In the standard oracle model, exact gradients expose only matrix-vector products with the precision matrix, leading to polynomial approximation barriers and a characteristic $\sqrt{\kappa}$ dependence on the known spectral range. We show that this barrier disappears when the sampler is allowed to query smoothed scores, namely gradients of the logarithms of the Gaussian-convolved densities. For a centered Gaussian target with precision matrix $\Lambda$, a smoothed-score query at noise level $\tau$ gives access to the resolvent $(\Lambda+\tau^{-1}I)^{-1}$. Combining geometrically spaced noise levels with sinc-quadrature rational approximation, we obtain a sampler with $q=O((\log\kappa+\log(e\sqrt d/\delta_{\rm TV}))\log(e\sqrt d/\delta_{\rm TV}))$ smoothed-score queries for total variation error $\delta_{\rm TV}$, improving the condition-number dependence from $\sqrt{\kappa}$ to logarithmic. We also study finite-bit gradient oracles. Using coordinatewise quantization of the transformed smoothed-score answers and a final dithering step, we obtain a sampling scheme whose total communicated gradient information is polylogarithmic in $\kappa$; in particular, for fixed dimension and accuracy, the bit complexity is $O(\log^2\kappa)$. To complement these upper bounds, we introduce a channel-synthesis, or reverse-Shannon, converse technique for sampling lower bounds. This converts total-variation simulation guarantees into communication requirements and yields an $\Omega(d\log\kappa)$ bit lower bound for $d\ge2$ and fixed total variation error below one, as $\kappa\to\infty$. Together, these results identify smoothed scores as a provably more informative oracle for sampling and give nearly matching upper and lower bounds for its finite-bit complexity.

entry.title: Soft-Radial Projection for Constrained End-to-End Learning

link.title: Soft-Radial Projection for Constrained End-to-End Learning

entry.content:
Constrained end-to-end learning trains neural networks whose outputs must satisfy feasibility constraints, such as resource, budget, or operational limits. While projection and optimization layers guarantee constraint satisfaction, boundary-based projections can introduce unfavorable optimization geometry: regions of the unconstrained output space are mapped to the same active face of the feasible set. This makes the resulting map locally rank-deficient, suppressing gradients in constrained directions and potentially impairing optimization - a bottleneck known as gradient saturation. We propose Soft-Radial Projection (SRP), a differentiable reparameterization layer that maps unconstrained network outputs into the relative interior of a convex feasible set by smoothly rescaling rays from a strictly feasible anchor point. Unlike hard radial or orthogonal projections, the resulting map is one-to-one and has a full-rank Jacobian almost everywhere, while guaranteeing strict feasibility. We prove that constrained networks equipped with SRP retain universal approximation guarantees. For polytopes and balls, the layer admits a closed-form forward pass, while for general convex sets, the ray-boundary intersection reduces to a one-dimensional search. Experiments on decision-focused learning benchmarks demonstrate strong solution quality at low computational cost, with particularly favorable results in portfolio optimization and substantially lower inference latency than differentiable optimization layers in the evaluated settings.

entry.title: Spatial fusion of DHS and MICS surveys with jittered and geomasked locations

link.title: Spatial fusion of DHS and MICS surveys with jittered and geomasked locations

entry.content:
In low- and middle-income countries, survey data is a key data source for public health monitoring. Not accounting for the anonymization applied to the GPS locations in these surveys may lead to bias, and in turn sub-optimal public health decision-making and outcomes. We propose a spatial fusion model to account both for jittering (a form of random perturbation of GPS coordinates) and geomasking (reporting only the name of the area containing the true GPS coordinates). This allows us to combine data from surveys with different kinds of positional uncertainty, reduce bias, and give more precise estimates. We use this approach to estimate women’s secondary education completion through a fusion model using both the 2018 Nigeria demographic and health survey (DHS), with jittered point locations, and the 2016 Nigeria multiple indicator cluster (MICS) survey, with geomasked locations. We show that accounting for the positional uncertainty in the surveys and accounting for both DHS and MICS surveys simultaneously can reduce bias while improving precision in parameter estimates and predictions via a simulation study and validation at cluster and areal levels. We recommend the proposed approach particularly in cases where the modeler wishes to model DHS and MICS surveys jointly, where continuously varying spatial covariates are used, and where local targeted spatial estimates are desired.

Read more

entry.title: Spatially varying quantile downscaling of summer temperature from atmospheric circulation and long-term trends over peninsular Spain

link.title: Spatially varying quantile downscaling of summer temperature from atmospheric circulation and long-term trends over peninsular Spain

entry.content:
Over recent decades, high temperatures have intensified worldwide, with impacts on human health, ecosystems, and the economy. Understanding their spatial evolution requires accounting for long-term temperature changes and the role of atmospheric circulation. Quantile regression provides a flexible framework for characterizing changes across the temperature distribution, with relevance to extremes. We analyze the spatio-temporal evolution of the 0.50 and 0.95 quantiles of daily maximum temperature during summer (June–August) over peninsular Spain from 1960 to 2023. We develop a Bayesian spatially varying quantile regression model for observations from 40 meteorological stations, using ERA5 geopotential fields at tropospheric levels to characterize atmospheric circulation, together with long-term temporal trends capturing the background climate change signal. The spatially varying coefficients allow the sensitivity of temperature to atmospheric circulation to differ across the region, linking synoptic dynamics with local temperature variability. The model separates changes associated with the dynamical atmospheric state from the long-term thermodynamic warming signal, while allowing their effects to vary across the temperature distribution. Results show that atmospheric circulation and long-term trends provide comparable contributions to the observed warming. Significant increases in median and upper-quantile temperatures are found across much of peninsular Spain, with pronounced heterogeneity across months and space, followed by quantiles

entry.title: Specification Testing for Dyadic Regression Models

link.title: Specification Testing for Dyadic Regression Models

entry.content:
Of the 88 empirical papers on dyadic or other relational data that we reviewed in the top five economics journals, 55 (62.5\%) use a linear specification. To assess whether such a specification describes the conditional mean, we develop Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cram'er-von Mises tests for undirected dyadic data that also accommodate smooth nonlinear specifications. To our knowledge, this paper is the first to develop omnibus specification tests for undirected dyadic regression models. A corrected first-order multiplier bootstrap is asymptotically exact in two standard Gaussian cases: the first-order nondegenerate case and independent dyads case. For a general class of such processes, we establish that a second-order multiplier bootstrap consistently approximates the limiting law uniformly over the indexing function class, even when the indexing functions are estimated. For the specification tests, we augment this bootstrap to account for two additional sources of non-Gaussianity: parameter estimation and the curvature of the regression function. We then construct an envelope test that is asymptotically exact in both Gaussian cases and controls size in the other degenerate cases. Simulations illustrate the size and power of the tests. In an application to housing sales, we reject a common mean price gap within distance bands but do not reject separate linear relationships by metro access.

Read more

entry.title: Spectral Graph Sparsification Preserves Representation Geometry in Graph Neural Networks

link.title: Spectral Graph Sparsification Preserves Representation Geometry in Graph Neural Networks

entry.content:
Spectral graph sparsification is a classical tool for reducing graph complexity while preserving Laplacian quadratic forms. In graph neural networks (GNNs), sparsification is often used to accelerate computation while maintaining predictive performance. In this work, we study a complementary representation-level question: does sparsification preserve the geometry of learned embeddings? For polynomial-filter GNNs, we prove that any $\epsilon$-spectral sparsifier induces $O(\epsilon)$ perturbations in polynomial graph filters, multilayer hidden representations, and their Gram matrices. These guarantees imply stability of squared pairwise distances, class means, and covariance structure in embedding space. We further establish finite-time training stability: under smoothness and boundedness assumptions, gradient descent on dense and sparsified graphs produces weight trajectories whose separation grows at most proportionally to the sparsification distortion. Empirically, effective-resistance sparsification validates the predicted perturbation chain on synthetic graphs and preserves hidden representation geometry on real datasets. In our experiments, the gram matrix and training dynamics show low divergence even under substantial sparsification, consistent with the predicted stability under spectral sparsification. Hidden Gram preservation strongly predicts neighborhood preservation and class-centroid stability across FashionMNIST, Cora, and Paul15. Together, these results show that spectral sparsification preserves not only graph operators, but also the representation geometry that supports downstream use of GNN embeddings for interpretability.

entry.title: Spectral Similarity Weights for Adaptive Conformal Prediction: A Bias-Variance Account and a Benchmark

link.title: Spectral Similarity Weights for Adaptive Conformal Prediction: A Bias-Variance Account and a Benchmark

entry.content:
Conformal prediction intervals lose their guarantee when a series is not exchangeable. We study weighting calibration residuals by the similarity of local Fourier power features, combined with the adaptive level update of ACI. A two-term account of the coverage error, mismatch that falls and sampling error that rises as the bandwidth shrinks, holds with exogenous features and conditionally independent residuals, but not for features computed from the series itself, which is how the method is used. In four simulations, spectral weighting lowered the mean regime-level deviation of coverage by 17% to 19% when the features came from the response and by 75% when they were exogenous, and not clearly under gradual drift. In each recurring-regime design a scaled-error baseline or Conformal PID control calibrated better. On nine public series with 36 forecast origins, spectral weighting with the plain weighted quantile did not differ from projected ACI in coverage error, and Conformal PID and scaled ACI were the best calibrated methods. The features are blind to seasonal phase, so the weights act like a recency kernel. A pure recency kernel did at least as well, especially with a finite-sample rank correction (mean absolute coverage error 0.039 against 0.090 for ACI; a post hoc check). Calendar phase weights narrowed German electricity intervals by 23% at equal coverage, but were not better than ACI across the series. We suggest trying adaptive baselines first, and similarity weights only where regimes differ in spectral shape or season and the effective sample size stays large.

entry.title: Spiking Sensory Networks

link.title: Spiking Sensory Networks

entry.content:
Effective sensory reception is critical for survival, yet the computational mechanisms behind how peripheral sensory neurons (SNs) transduce external signals into spiking representations for downstream brain circuits remain to be fully understood. Numerous theoretical frameworks have been proposed to model sensory processing, with Bayesian approaches among the most prominent. However, existing machine learning attempts to apply Bayesian theory to spiking neurons remain largely phenomenological, disconnected from empirical biology, and poorly validated on non-stationary temporal data. Conversely, neuroscientific models often rely on strong inductive experimental biases or explicit kinetic dynamics fit post hoc to match spiking data. Here, we introduce a class of recurrent Poisson VAE models, termed Spiking Sensory Networks (SSNs), that bridge these paradigms by reconciling variational inference with biologically inspired spike transduction for time-varying stimuli. Evaluated on real-world odor plume recordings from locust olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), SSNs match or exceed the reconstruction fidelity of Spiking Neural Network (SNN) and GLM baselines while exhibiting superior representational characteristics. Furthermore, SSNs are well-suited for neuroscientific investigation, learning empirical in vivo ORN response motifs and exhibiting emergent spike-frequency adaptation under unsupervised reconstruction without manual tuning. Moreover, we theoretically link the recurrent decoding objective to mutual information maximization, and derive a formal thermodynamic lower bound connecting the Poisson Kullback-Leibler regularizer to the excess non-equilibrium metabolic power of biophysical homeostasis. Ultimately, our work synthesizes principles from machine learning theory and empirical neuroscience, providing a viable bridge that concretizes Bayesian models with biological mechanisms.

entry.title: Stable GFlowNets with TV Monitoring and Probabilistic Guarantees

link.title: Stable GFlowNets with TV Monitoring and Probabilistic Guarantees

entry.content:
Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) sample diverse structured objects in proportion to reward and have been applied to molecular discovery and biological-sequence design, where finding multiple high-quality candidates is more useful than returning a single optimum. Despite their theoretical promise, practical training is often unstable, exhibiting severe loss spikes and mode collapse. To address this, we first assess the sensitivity of GFlowNet objectives, demonstrating that a small Total Variation (TV) distance between the learned and target distributions does not preclude an unbounded training loss. Motivated by this mismatch, we establish converse guarantees by deriving loss-to-TV bounds that certify global fidelity from bounded trajectory balance losses. Lastly, we propose Stable GFlowNets, which leverages our theory to stabilize training via adaptive reference flow and improves the trade-off among mode coverage, robustness, and certifiability. Code is available at: https://github.com/tjleizeng/StableGFlowNets.

Read more

entry.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects

link.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects

entry.content:
Whether an action-conditioned world model uses actions is usually checked by replacing or removing them and measuring lost accuracy. With biological experiments as the guiding case, we show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. A second failure is specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle’s rose. Our preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx1.1\times10^{10}$). Tempering factors estimated from residuals can err by an order of magnitude, whereas a mixture over a fixed grid of factors needs no estimate and loses at most the logarithm of the grid size in log e-value relative to its best member. In a registered test on a diffusion world model for three Atari games released by others, the pooled test rejected in 0 of 96 units in which actions mattered and Kish and contrast tempering in 0 and 1, while the mixture rejected in 96; under an exact null, eight statistics made 0 rejections in 1,536 tests. Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol, or labelled exploratory.

entry.title: Statistical Inference for Rates of Change in Spatial Processes over Riemannian Manifolds

link.title: Statistical Inference for Rates of Change in Spatial Processes over Riemannian Manifolds

entry.content:
Statistical inference for spatial processes from partially realized or scattered data has seen voluminous developments in diverse areas ranging from environmental sciences to business and economics. Inference on the associated rates of change has seen some recent developments. The literature has been restricted to Euclidean domains, where inference is sought on directional derivatives, rates along a chosen direction of interest, at arbitrary locations. Inference for higher order rates, particularly directional curvature has also proved useful in these settings. Modern spatial data often arise from non-Euclidean domains. This manuscript particularly considers spatial processes defined over compact Riemannian manifolds. We develop a comprehensive inferential framework for spatial rates of change for such processes over vector fields. In doing so, we formalize smoothness of process realizations and construct differential processes – the derivative and curvature processes. We derive conditions for kernels that ensure the existence of these processes and establish validity of the joint multivariate process consisting of the ``parent’’ Gaussian process (GP) over the manifold and the associated differential processes. Predictive inference on these rates is devised conditioned on the realized process over the manifold. Manifolds arise as polyhedral meshes in practice. The success of our simulation experiments for assessing derivatives for processes observed over such meshes validate our theoretical findings. By enhancing our understanding of GPs on manifolds, this manuscript unlocks a variety of potential applications in machine learning and statistics where GPs have seen wide usage. We propose a fully model-based approach to inference on the differential processes arising from a spatial process from partially observed or realized data across scattered location on a manifold.

entry.title: Statopia: A Prover–Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics

link.title: Statopia: A Prover–Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics

entry.content:
Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops Statopia Prover, an independent agent specialized for formalizing and proving results in statistics and machine learning, and Statlib, a Lean~4 library built with the prover and organized for automated use. The prover controls its own execution without relying on external coding agents. It is built for formal proof discovery and checking existing proofs. A natural-language proof, when available, guides its search but is not required: from a statement alone, the prover develops the argument itself and constructs a Lean proof. Its workflow integrates source preparation, statement review, library supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable proof development. Statlib’s shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and its coverage of statistics keeps expanding. Verified results and usage feedback from the prover inform reviewed library updates, so that proof development drives this expansion. A cross-platform application provides an interactive workspace for uploading source files and running tasks locally or in the cloud.

Statlib’s shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and its coverage of statistics keeps expanding. Verified results and usage feedback from the prover inform reviewed library updates, so that proof development drives this expansion. A cross-platform application provides an interactive workspace for uploading source files and running tasks locally or in the cloud.

entry.title: Streaming robust covariance estimation and sequential outlier detection

link.title: Streaming robust covariance estimation and sequential outlier detection

entry.content:
Robust estimation of the covariance matrix and outlier detection remain major statistical hurdles, particularly in large datasets where the rate of data contamination increases. The presence of outliers can severely bias parameter estimates and induce a masking effect, whereby some outliers conceal the presence of other outliers, further complicating their detection. Although many approaches have been proposed for covariance estimation and outlier detection, to our knowledge, none of these methods have been implemented in an online setting. In this paper, we focus on online covariance matrix estimation and outlier detection. Specifically, we propose a new method for simultaneously and online estimating the geometric median and variance, which allows us to calculate the Mahalanobis distance for each incoming data point before deciding whether it should be considered an outlier. To mitigate the masking effect, robust estimation techniques for the mean and variance are required. Our approach uses the geometric median for robust estimation of the location and the median covariance matrix for robust estimation of the dispersion parameters. The new online methods proposed for parameter estimation and outlier detection allow real-time identification of outliers as data are observed sequentially. The performance of our methods is demonstrated on simulated and real datasets.

Read more

entry.title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning with Time-Varying Movement Costs

link.title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning with Time-Varying Movement Costs

entry.content:
We study online convex optimization (OCO) with time-varying movement costs, where the learner incurs both a loss and a time-dependent penalty for changing its decisions. While previous work has established dynamic regret guarantees for this setting, obtaining strongly adaptive guarantees that hold simultaneously over arbitrary intervals remains an open challenge. We address this by developing a new algorithm which, for every interval $[a,b]\subseteq[T]$ and arbitrary comparator sequence, achieves a data-dependent regret bound of $ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \sqrt{(D^2+DP_{[a,b]})\sum_{t \in [a,b]}(|g_t|^2+\lambda_t|g_t|)} \right) $, where $D$ is the diameter of the decision domain, $P_{[a,b]}$ is the path length of the comparator sequence over $[a,b]$, $g_t$ is the gradient of the loss, and $\lambda_t$ is the movement-cost coefficient at round~$t$. Key to our approach is a novel reduction to sleeping experts with movement costs, a previously unexplored variant that is of independent interest. As a result of our development, we further obtain strongly-adaptive dynamic regret guarantees under arbitrary delayed feedback with a refined dependence on interval-restricted cumulative delays. Our approach also naturally extends to OCO with time-varying memory, where we obtain strongly-adaptive guarantees which improve the best-known bounds.

Read more

entry.title: Structure-Adaptive Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Kernel Methods

link.title: Structure-Adaptive Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Kernel Methods

entry.content:
We study conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimation from observational data in regimes with potentially weak overlap, when the nuisance response functions lie in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), but the contrast function is structurally simpler. We consider three forms of such simplicity: (i) membership in a lower-complexity RKHS with faster eigenvalue decay, (ii) a source condition relative to the nuisance kernel, or (iii) dependence on a known low-dimensional covariate representation. We develop a unified two-stage kernel ridge regression procedure that remains valid under weak overlap and attains minimax rates determined by the complexity of the contrast function. The procedure avoids propensity-score estimation and separate nuisance convergence-rate assumptions. We also show that a simple model-selection step over candidate contrast spaces and regularization levels satisfies an oracle inequality, enabling adaptation to unknown CATE regularity.

Read more

entry.title: TOPPO: Rethinking PPO for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Critic Balancing

link.title: TOPPO: Rethinking PPO for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Critic Balancing

entry.content:
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and its variants dominate Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) due to their off-policy sample efficiency, while on-policy methods such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remain underexplored. We diagnose that PPO in MTRL suffers from a previously overlooked issue: critic-side gradient ill-conditioning, which may cause tail tasks to stall while easy tasks dominate the value function’s updates. To address this, we propose TOPPO (Tail-Optimized PPO), a reformulation of PPO via Critic Balancing – a set of modules that improve gradient conditioning and balance learning dynamics across tasks. Unlike prior approaches that rely on modular architectures or large models, TOPPO targets the optimization bottleneck within PPO itself. Empirically, on the Meta-World+ MT50 benchmark, TOPPO achieves stronger mean and tail-task performance than prior SAC-family and ARS-family methods while using substantially fewer parameters and reaching their final performance in fewer environment steps. Notably, TOPPO matches or surpasses strong SAC baselines early in training and maintains superior performance at full budget. Ablations confirm the effectiveness of each module in TOPPO and provide insights into their interactions. Our results demonstrate that, with proper optimization, on-policy methods can rival or exceed off-policy approaches in MTRL, challenging the prevailing reliance on SAC and highlighting critic-side gradient conditioning as the central bottleneck.

Read more

entry.title: TRACE: Adaptive Credibility Reweighting for Robust Bayesian Model Selection with Source Summary Statistics

link.title: TRACE: Adaptive Credibility Reweighting for Robust Bayesian Model Selection with Source Summary Statistics

entry.content:
This study focuses on regression estimation and variable selection based on target data, while incorporating information from coefficient estimates obtained in related studies. A weighted combination of these estimates may agree with some target effects but differ from others. We propose Transfer Regression with Adaptive Credibility Estimation (TRACE), a Bayesian method requiring only fitted coefficients and sample sizes from source studies. TRACE learns simplex-constrained source weights shared across variables. Separate latent indicators determine target inclusion and whether each coefficient is guided by the weighted source estimate. We develop an approximate collapsed variational expectation-maximization algorithm with robust source-weight initialization. Under suitable conditions, consistency of variable selection, transfer decisions, and source-weight estimation is established. These results hold at every prespecified fixed iteration in fixed dimension and at global mean-field optima of the exact collapsed variational objective as the dimension grows. Simulations show that TRACE achieves competitive variable-selection performance under different patterns of source heterogeneity. An application to data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression project illustrates its use in cross-tissue gene-expression prediction.

Read more

entry.title: Tail behaviour of infimum of Gaussian processes

link.title: Tail behaviour of infimum of Gaussian processes

entry.content:
We investigate the upper tail of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$, where $X$ is a centred Gaussian process (GP) with continuous sample paths on a nonempty compact metric space $\mathcal T$. As suggested by the findings of [1], the exponential rate is governed by an optimal-measure problem, while the exact prefactor depends on the local geometry of the corresponding contact set. In the full-contact regime, we strengthen the known Gumbel max-domain of attraction property of the distribution of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$ by establishing the von Mises condition. For fractional Brownian motion on $[a,b]$, $0u}$ as $u\to\infty$ under suitable local assumptions. We illustrate our findings with examples including fractional Brownian motion and the fractional Brownian sheet.

entry.title: Task Vector Geometry Underlies Dual Modes of Task Inference in Transformers

link.title: Task Vector Geometry Underlies Dual Modes of Task Inference in Transformers

entry.content:
Transformers are effective at inferring the latent task from context via two inference modes: recognizing a task seen during training, and adapting to a novel one. Recent interpretability studies have identified from middle-layer representations task-specific directions, or task vectors, that steer model behavior. However, a lack of rigorous foundations hinders connecting internal representations to external model behavior: existing work fails to explain how task-vector geometry is shaped by the training distribution, and what geometry enables out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. In this paper, we study these questions in a controlled synthetic setting by training small transformers from scratch on latent-task sequence distributions, which allows a principled mathematical characterization. We show that two inference modes can coexist within a single model. In-distribution behavior is governed by Bayesian task retrieval, implemented internally through convex combinations of learned task vectors. OOD behavior, by contrast, arises through extrapolative task learning, whose representations occupy a subspace nearly orthogonal to the task-vector subspace. Taken together, our results suggest that task-vector geometry, training distributions, and generalization behaviors are closely related.

Read more
